title: Viruses, vaccines, prions and viroids: how a cell is taken over, and how a body gets ready

summary.text: A virus has no hands, no engine and no food of their own. So how does one virus particle turn a healthy cell into a place that makes thousands of new viruses? In this lesson you will run a model cell with marked grains to see whose jobs get done, test whether changed milk can change fresh milk, and play a card game in which a body with a vaccine meets a virus. You will also meet prions and viroids, which are copied with even less than a virus has.
summary.art: A cut-away drawing of a round cell with small work stations inside, most of them building tiny virus particles and only a few building the cell's own parts.

intro.hook: A polio virus particle is a small ball of protein with one strand of instructions inside. They cannot move by themselves, and they cannot build anything. Yet four to six hours after one particle enters a cell, that cell can release up to 10,000 new ones. Who built them?
intro.text: The cell built them. The virus brought only a message, and the cell's own builders read the message and did the work. In this lesson you will find out why a cell does this, why you feel fine for a day or two after a virus gets in, and how a vaccine uses the same facts to get your body ready. Then you will meet two things that are copied with even less: a prion, which is one wrongly folded protein, and a viroid, which is one bare loop of RNA.
intro.art: One tiny ball-shaped virus particle beside a large cell on the left, and on the right the same cell with thousands of identical tiny balls pouring out.

outcomes: By the end I can explain how a virus takes over a cell: the cell's own ribosomes build from the virus's messages.
By the end I can explain why a person feels well for some time after a virus gets in, and name three ways a virus carries on: burst, bud or hide.
By the end I can describe how a cell warns the cells nearby with interferon, and how bacteria remember viruses.
By the end I can explain what a vaccine shows the body, and name four kinds of vaccine with an example of each.
By the end I can explain why some vaccines protect for many years, why the flu vaccine changes, and why some viruses have no vaccine yet.
By the end I can say what a prion and a viroid are, and how each gets copied.
By the end I can run a model with a fair test, and say what the model shows and what it leaves out.

terms.meaning: The living cell that a virus enters and is copied in.
terms.example: A cell in the lining of your nose is the host cell of a cold virus.
terms.art: A row of nose-lining cells with one cell highlighted and a tiny virus particle touching that cell's surface.

terms.meaning: A protein on the outside of a cell that the cell uses to take things in or to receive signals. A virus can enter only if part of their coat fits a receptor.
terms.example: A polio virus fits a receptor found on the cells of humans and some monkeys, so polio does not infect dogs or cows.
terms.art: A close-up of a cell surface with a cup-shaped receptor and a virus spike that fits into it exactly.

terms.meaning: The full set of instructions that a living being carries, written in DNA or RNA.
terms.example: The genome of a polio virus is one strand of RNA about 7,500 letters long. Yours is about 3,000 million letters of DNA.
terms.art: A short thread labelled 7,500 letters beside a huge ball of thread labelled 3,000 million letters.

terms.meaning: A short working copy of one instruction. A cell makes it from a gene, and a ribosome reads it to build one protein.
terms.example: When a skin cell needs more keratin, the cell copies the keratin gene into mRNA and sends the mRNA to the ribosomes.
terms.art: A long DNA thread inside a nucleus with a short strand peeling off it and travelling out to a small ribosome.

terms.meaning: A tiny builder inside every cell. It reads a message of mRNA and joins amino acids into the protein that the message describes.
terms.example: One human cell has millions of ribosomes. A virus particle has none.
terms.art: A small two-part blob sitting on a strand of mRNA, with a chain of beads growing out of its top.

terms.meaning: A long chain of amino acids, folded into an exact shape. The shape decides what the protein can do.
terms.example: The keratin in your hair, the haemoglobin in your blood and the coat of a virus are all proteins.
terms.art: A string of coloured beads on the left and the same string folded into a neat compact shape on the right.

terms.meaning: What happens when a cell's ribosomes and materials are used to make virus parts in place of the cell's own parts.
terms.example: A few hours after a polio virus enters a cell, that cell is building almost nothing but virus proteins.
terms.art: A cell in which nearly every ribosome holds a strand marked with a small V, and only two hold a plain strand.

terms.meaning: The number of new virus particles that one infected cell releases.
terms.example: A bacterium infected by lambda phage releases about 100 new phages. A cell infected by polio virus can release up to 10,000.
terms.art: A split-open bacterium with about a hundred tiny phage particles spilling out.

terms.meaning: The time between a germ getting in and the first sign of illness.
terms.example: A cold shows after about one to three days. During that time the virus is being copied, but there are too few infected cells for you to feel anything.
terms.art: A calendar strip of four days with a tiny virus on day one and a sneezing child on day three.

terms.meaning: A virus whose genome stays quietly inside a cell, sometimes for many years, without new particles being made.
terms.example: After chickenpox, the virus stays latent in nerve cells beside the spine. Decades later they can wake and cause shingles.
terms.art: A nerve cell body with a small quiet loop of virus genome inside the nucleus and a clock beside it.

terms.meaning: A virus who infects bacteria.
terms.example: Lambda phage infects the gut bacterium E. coli. Esther Lederberg found lambda in 1950.
terms.art: A phage with a many-sided head and a tail standing on the surface of a rod-shaped bacterium.

terms.meaning: A signal protein that an infected cell releases. It warns the cells nearby, and they slow down their own protein building so that a virus gains less.
terms.example: The aches and tiredness of flu come partly from your own interferon and similar signals, and not only from the virus.
terms.art: One infected cell sending out small dots that reach three neighbouring cells, which grow a thicker outline.

terms.meaning: Any part of a germ that the body's defenders can recognise by its shape.
terms.example: The spike on the outside of the Covid virus is an antigen. Covid vaccines show the body this spike.
terms.art: A virus particle with one of the outer spikes circled and drawn larger beside it.

terms.meaning: A Y-shaped protein made by white blood cells called B cells. Its tips fit one antigen and stick to it.
terms.example: Antibodies that fit a measles virus's coat cover the coat, so the virus no longer fits the cell's receptor.
terms.art: Several small Y shapes stuck all over a virus particle, covering the spikes.

terms.meaning: A white blood cell that stays in the body for years after an infection or a vaccine, and can quickly make the right antibodies again.
terms.example: A person who had measles as a child still carries memory cells for measles at seventy.
terms.art: A round white blood cell sitting quietly in a lymph node, holding a small card with a virus spike drawn on it.

terms.meaning: A safe preparation that shows the body an antigen of a germ, so that memory cells are ready before the real germ arrives.
terms.example: The measles vaccine is given to babies in India at nine months and again in the second year.
terms.art: A health worker giving an injection in the upper arm of a baby held by a parent.

terms.meaning: A vaccine made of a living virus that has been changed so that the virus multiplies a little and does not cause the disease. The other word for weakened is attenuated.
terms.example: The measles vaccine, the oral polio drops and the Indian rotavirus vaccine Rotavac are live weakened vaccines.
terms.art: Two drops falling from a small dropper into the open mouth of a baby.

terms.meaning: A vaccine made of whole virus particles that have been treated with a chemical or heat, so that they can no longer be copied.
terms.example: Covaxin, made in Hyderabad, is an inactivated Covid vaccine. The injected polio vaccine is another.
terms.art: A vial beside a drawing of whole virus particles, each with a broken thread inside.

terms.meaning: A vaccine that carries the message for one virus protein. Your own ribosomes read the message and build that one protein, and your defenders learn its shape.
terms.example: Two of the Covid vaccines used across the world from 2020 were mRNA vaccines.
terms.art: A tiny fat bubble holding a short strand of mRNA, entering a cell where a ribosome builds one spike.

terms.meaning: The slow change in a virus's antigens as copying mistakes build up, until old antibodies fit less well.
terms.example: Flu viruses drift so fast that the World Health Organization chooses new strains for the flu vaccine twice a year.
terms.art: A row of five virus spikes, each a little different in shape from the one before, with an antibody that fits only the first.

terms.meaning: Ending a disease everywhere in the world, so that nobody catches it any more.
terms.example: Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980. India's last case of wild polio was on 13 January 2011.
terms.art: A world map with a single last red dot being crossed out.

terms.meaning: A protein that has folded into a wrong shape and makes normal proteins of the same kind take the wrong shape too. A prion has no DNA or RNA.
terms.example: Mad cow disease and kuru are prion diseases of the brain.
terms.art: A neat coiled protein beside a flat, folded-over version of the same protein that is pressing against it.

terms.meaning: A bare loop of RNA, a few hundred letters long, with no coat and no gene for any protein. Viroids are known only in plants.
terms.example: The coconut cadang-cadang viroid is 246 letters long. They have killed more than 30 million coconut palms in the Philippines.
terms.art: A tiny closed loop of thread, pinched into a rod shape, inside a plant cell near the nucleus.

terms.meaning: A stretch of DNA in which a bacterium stores short pieces of the viruses who attacked their ancestors. The bacterium uses the pieces to recognise and cut the same virus later.
terms.example: The bacteria that make yoghurt resist a phage better after they have stored a piece of that phage's DNA.
terms.art: A circular bacterial chromosome with a short striped section, each stripe labelled as a piece of a different phage.

explanations.concept: What taking over means: the cell builds the virus
explanations.definition: A virus takes over a cell when the cell's ribosomes build virus proteins from the virus's messages, and the cell's enzymes and materials are used to copy the virus genome.
explanations.description: A cell is always building. The cell's genes are copied into short messages called mRNA, and millions of ribosomes read those messages and build proteins. A ribosome builds from any message that has the right starting signal. It does not turn a message away because of where the message came from. This is the fact a virus depends on. When a virus genome gets into a cell, messages made from that genome join the cell's own messages. Ribosomes meet messages by bumping into them. So the more virus messages there are, the more often a ribosome picks one up. At the same time the virus genome is copied again and again, so the virus messages multiply while the cell's messages do not. After a few hours most of the building in the cell is for the virus. Nothing was forced. The virus brought instructions, and the cell supplied the ribosomes, the amino acids, the energy and the work. This is a simplified picture. A real cell has millions of ribosomes, and each virus has extra ways to get ahead. But the main point holds for every virus.
examples: A polio virus particle carries one strand of RNA about 7,500 letters long. The cell's ribosomes read that strand directly, as if it were one of the cell's own messages.
In the Factory Test, you drew six grains each round and built whatever each one said. The marked grains doubled each round, so more and more of your six jobs were for the virus.
An mRNA vaccine works because of the same fact. Your ribosomes build the spike protein from a message that your own genes never wrote.
explanations.art: A ribosome in the middle with two message strands approaching it, one plain and one marked with a small V, and the same chain of beads starting to grow from either.
explanations.context: This card explains what it means for a virus to take over a cell, and why a cell builds the virus at all.

explanations.concept: The quiet gap: why nothing seems to happen at first
explanations.definition: For some time after a virus enters a cell, no finished virus particle can be found in that cell. In a body, the same gap shows as the incubation period, when the person is infected and feels well.
explanations.description: In 1939, Emory Ellis and Max Delbrück added phages to bacteria and counted the phages every few minutes. They expected the number to climb steadily. It did not. For a stretch of time the count stayed flat, and then it jumped all at once. The phages had been copied in one step, inside the bacteria, and released together when the bacteria burst. Later work showed something stranger. If you break open an infected cell early, you find no whole virus inside at all. The particle that went in has come apart, and the new ones are not yet put together. Scientists call this hidden stretch the eclipse. In lambda phage the first new particle appears about 20 minutes after infection, and the bacterium bursts at about 50 minutes. The same thing happens in your body on a larger scale. One infected nose cell is far too few to notice. The virus must go through several rounds of cells before enough cells are infected, and before your own alarm signals make you feel ill. So a person can pass a cold on a day before they sneeze.
examples: In the Factory Test, rounds 1, 2 and 3 usually gave no virus jobs or just one. The virus was in the cell and doubling the whole time.
A cell infected with polio virus looks normal for the first hours. It breaks open four to six hours after the virus got in.
A cold shows about one to three days after the virus gets in. Chickenpox takes about two weeks.
explanations.art: A line graph that lies flat along the bottom for a long stretch and then jumps straight up in one step, with a small bacterium drawn under the flat part and a burst bacterium under the jump.
explanations.context: This card explains why nothing seems to happen for a while after a virus gets into a cell, or into a person.

explanations.concept: How some viruses make sure their own messages are read first
explanations.definition: Many viruses do more than add messages. They block, cut or steal from the cell's own messages, so that the ribosomes are left with mostly virus messages to read.
explanations.description: If a virus only added messages, the virus would have to share the ribosomes with the cell. Many viruses do better than that. Most of a cell's messages carry a small chemical cap at the front end. The cap is how a ribosome finds the start. Polio virus messages have no cap. They have a folded stretch of RNA that lets a ribosome start in the middle. Soon after infection, the cell's capped messages stop being read, while the virus's messages still are. Within hours the cell is building almost nothing but polio proteins. Flu viruses do it another way. A flu enzyme cuts the caps off the cell's own messages and sticks them onto flu messages. Scientists call this cap snatching. The cell's message is ruined, and the flu message now looks like the cell's own. Some viruses simply make so many messages that the cell's are crowded out. Each trick is different, but each does the same job. It makes sure that the cell's ribosomes spend their time on the virus.
examples: Polio virus: the cell's own protein building is shut down, and the virus's messages are read by a different way of starting.
Flu virus: the caps are cut from the cell's messages and reused on the virus's messages.
In the Factory Test you can add this rule: take out two plain grains every round. The virus then wins the ribosomes sooner.
explanations.art: Two message strands side by side, the plain one with its front tip snipped off by tiny scissors and the tip being fixed onto the strand marked V.
explanations.context: This card explains the extra tricks that viruses such as polio and flu use, so that a cell reads the virus's messages before the cell's own.

explanations.concept: Three ways to carry on: burst, bud or hide
explanations.definition: New virus particles leave a cell by bursting the cell or by budding out through the cell's membrane. Some viruses also stay hidden in the cell as a quiet genome and are copied only when the cell divides or when they wake.
explanations.description: Once new particles are assembled, they have to get out. Polio viruses and many phages burst the cell, and the cell dies. Flu viruses bud. Each new particle pushes out through the cell's membrane and leaves wrapped in a piece of it. The cell can go on releasing flu particles for hours before dying. The third way is to wait. In 1950, Esther Lederberg at the University of Wisconsin was growing a strain of the gut bacterium E. coli that had been treated with ultraviolet light. When she mixed this strain with the original, untreated strain, clear holes appeared in the layer of bacteria. Holes like that are made by phages. But she had added no phage. She worked out that the original strain had been carrying a phage all along, joined into the bacteria's own DNA and copied quietly at every division. The treated strain had lost theirs, so they had no protection. She named the phage lambda. Lambda senses the state of the cell. In a well-fed cell they usually burst out. In a starving cell they usually join the cell's DNA and wait. If the cell's DNA is damaged, they wake and leave. Viruses of humans hide too. The chickenpox virus stays in nerve cells for life. HIV writes a DNA copy of their genome into the DNA of white blood cells, which is why HIV is so hard to clear.
examples: Burst: polio virus, and lambda phage in a well-fed bacterium, with about 100 new phages from each cell.
Bud: flu virus and HIV, each particle wrapped in a piece of the cell's own membrane.
Hide: lambda in a starving bacterium, the chickenpox virus in nerve cells, and HIV in white blood cells.
explanations.art: Three cells in a row: the first split open with particles flying out, the second with small bubbles pinching off the surface, and the third whole and calm with a short marked stretch inside the DNA.
explanations.context: This card explains the three things a virus can do after entering a cell: burst out, bud out, or stay hidden for a long time.

explanations.concept: The cell fights back: interferon, the first alarm
explanations.definition: An infected cell releases signal proteins called interferons. Cells nearby respond by slowing their own protein building and by cutting up RNA, so that a virus who enters them gains much less.
explanations.description: A cell is not helpless. Cells carry sensors for things that should not be there, such as long double strands of RNA, which many viruses make while being copied. When a sensor finds one, the cell does two things. The cell sends out interferon and begins to shut down. Interferon drifts to the cells nearby and fits receptors on them. Those cells have not met the virus yet, but they get ready. They make one enzyme that slows all protein building, and another that cuts up RNA. Both hurt the cell a little. But a cell that builds slowly is a poor factory for a virus. Interferon also pushes badly infected cells to destroy themselves, which ends the virus's copying in that cell. Alick Isaacs and Jean Lindenmann described interferon in London in 1957. They named it for the way it interferes with virus copying. This alarm works within hours, long before any antibody is made. It is also the reason for much of what you feel. The fever, the aches and the tiredness of flu come partly from interferon and similar signals. So feeling ill is partly your own defence at work.
examples: A cell next to an infected cell slows their ribosomes after receiving interferon, even though no virus has reached them yet.
An infected cell who self-destructs early releases few or no new virus particles.
In the Factory Test, the 'alarm' rule is to take out two marked grains each round before copying. With one starting grain the virus is cleared at once.
explanations.art: One cell with a virus inside sending out a ring of small dots, and the neighbouring cells drawn with half their ribosomes resting.
explanations.context: This card explains how a cell that has been infected warns the cells nearby, hours before the body makes any antibodies.

explanations.definition: Many bacteria keep short pieces of the DNA of phages who attacked them, stored in a part of their own genome called CRISPR. They use the pieces to recognise the same phage later and cut that phage's DNA.
explanations.description: Phages have attacked bacteria for billions of years, and bacteria have many defences. One of them is a kind of memory. When a phage injects DNA into a bacterium, the bacterium sometimes cuts out a short piece of that DNA and stores it in a row with other pieces. The row is called CRISPR. The bacterium copies each stored piece into a short guide RNA. A cutting protein called Cas carries the guide around the cell. If DNA matching the guide ever turns up, Cas cuts it. Because the row is part of the bacterium's own DNA, it is copied at every division. So the daughters inherit the memory. In 2007, Rodolphe Barrangou and his team showed this in the bacteria that make yoghurt. Bacteria that survived a phage attack had added a new piece matching that phage, and they now resisted the phage. About half of all bacteria whose genomes have been read have CRISPR. In 2012, Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna showed how to give Cas a guide of their own choosing, so that it cuts any DNA they pick. They received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020. The gene-editing tool used in laboratories today began as a bacterium's memory of a virus.
examples: Streptococcus thermophilus, a yoghurt bacterium, stores pieces of the phages that spoil yoghurt cultures.
A bacterium's stored pieces are in the order the attacks came, so the row is a record of that family's past infections.
Your memory cells are not passed to your children. A bacterium's CRISPR row is.
explanations.art: A bacterium with a small scissor-shaped protein holding a short guide strand up against an incoming phage DNA thread, and behind it a row of short striped pieces in the bacterium's chromosome.
explanations.context: This card explains how bacteria keep a record of the viruses who attacked them, and how that record became a tool for editing genes.

explanations.concept: What a vaccine shows the body
explanations.definition: A vaccine shows the body an antigen of a germ without the disease. The body makes antibodies and memory cells that fit the antigen, so the response to the real germ starts days earlier.
explanations.description: Your body's defenders recognise a virus by shape. They do not need the whole virus, and they do not need the virus to be dangerous. They need to meet the shape of some part of the virus, called an antigen. The first time B cells meet a new antigen, it takes about one to two weeks before large amounts of well-fitting antibody are made. During those weeks the virus is doubling. After the first meeting, some of the cells that fit stay on as memory cells. If the same antigen appears again, they respond within a few days, with more antibody and a better fit. A vaccine is a first meeting arranged on purpose. This matters because of the quiet gap. A virus needs several rounds of copying before the person is ill. If antibodies arrive during the gap, they cover the virus particles as they leave each cell, and the particles no longer fit their receptor. The infection ends while it is still small. So a vaccinated person may still be infected for a short time. The vaccine changes the timing. It does not put up a wall.
examples: In Seven Steps or Stopped, the body with a vaccine starts with antibody cards in hand. The body without one starts with no cards and draws them slowly.
A child who has had two doses of measles vaccine and meets measles usually never knows it.
The vaccine against rabies can be given after a dog bite, because the rabies virus takes weeks to reach the brain.
explanations.art: Two timelines one above the other: on the top one a virus curve rises high before an antibody curve begins, and on the bottom one the antibody curve begins early and the virus curve stays low.
explanations.context: This card explains what a vaccine does: it lets the body meet the shape of a germ early, so that the real germ is met in time.

explanations.definition: A vaccine can show the body a live weakened virus, a whole inactivated virus, one part of a virus, or the instructions for making one part.
explanations.description: Every vaccine has to show the body an antigen. There are four main ways to do it. The first is a live weakened virus. The virus multiplies a little in the body, so one or two doses give strong, long protection. The measles vaccine, the oral polio drops and Rotavac are of this kind. The second is a whole virus that has been inactivated with a chemical, so that the genome can no longer be copied. The shape is still there. Covaxin is of this kind, and so is the injected polio vaccine. These usually need more doses, because nothing multiplies. The third shows only a part. The hepatitis B vaccine holds one protein from the virus's surface. Since 1986 that protein has been made by yeast cells that were given the virus's gene for it. It was the first human vaccine made by moving a gene into another cell. The fourth kind gives instructions and lets your own cells build the part. Covishield does this with a harmless chimpanzee cold virus that carries the gene for the Covid spike. An mRNA vaccine does it with the message alone. Each kind has costs. Live vaccines are strong but are not given to people whose defences are very weak. Part-only vaccines are very safe but need boosters.
examples: Live weakened: measles, oral polio drops, and Rotavac, the Indian rotavirus vaccine licensed in 2014.
Whole inactivated: Covaxin, made by Bharat Biotech with the National Institute of Virology, and the injected polio vaccine.
One part: hepatitis B. Instructions: Covishield, made in Pune, and the mRNA Covid vaccines.
explanations.art: Four small panels in a row: a whole virus with a smiling weak look, a whole virus with a broken thread inside, a single spike on its own, and a short message strand inside a fat bubble.
explanations.context: This card explains the four main kinds of vaccine and gives Indian examples of each.

explanations.concept: A message as a vaccine: the work of Katalin Karikó
explanations.definition: An mRNA vaccine is a message for one virus protein, wrapped in a tiny bubble of fat. Cells take it in, their ribosomes build the protein, and the body's defenders learn its shape. The message breaks down within days.
explanations.description: If ribosomes build from any message, then a message could be a medicine. Katalin Karikó, a biochemist born in Hungary in 1955, worked on this idea for decades. There was a serious problem. Cells have sensors for RNA that comes from outside, because that is what many viruses are. When mRNA made in a laboratory was put into the body, the sensors raised the alarm, and the mRNA was destroyed before it could be read. Her grant requests were turned down again and again, and in 1995 the University of Pennsylvania demoted her. She kept working. In 2005 she and the immunologist Drew Weissman found the answer. RNA has four kinds of letter. They swapped one of them, uridine, for a slightly different form called pseudouridine, which cells also use in some of their own RNA. The sensors now stayed quiet, and the ribosomes still read the message. Two leading journals rejected the paper before a third one published it. When Covid arrived in 2020, vaccines built on this finding were ready within a year. Karikó and Weissman received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2023. An mRNA vaccine does not enter the nucleus and does not change DNA. It is read for a short time and then broken down, like any other message.
examples: The mRNA in a Covid vaccine is the message for the spike protein only. No other part of the virus is made.
mRNA is fragile, so the message travels inside a tiny bubble of fat, and the vaccine is stored very cold.
The same method is being tested for vaccines against flu and for treatments made for one patient's cancer.
explanations.art: A woman scientist at a laboratory bench holding up a small tube, with a drawing beside her of a message strand in which one letter is circled and swapped.
explanations.context: This card tells how Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman made it possible to use a message of mRNA as a vaccine.

explanations.concept: Why some vaccines last and some must change
explanations.definition: A vaccine protects for as long as the virus's antigens stay the same and the body's memory lasts. Viruses whose antigens change quickly, or who come in very many types, are hard or impossible to vaccinate against so far.
explanations.description: Two doses of measles vaccine are about 97 percent effective, and the protection lasts for many years. The flu vaccine is remade every year and is about 40 to 60 percent effective in an average year. Why are they so different? Both viruses make copying mistakes at a high rate. The difference lies in what the mistakes do. The part of the measles virus that fits the cell's receptor seems to tolerate almost no change. A measles virus with a changed coat usually can no longer enter cells. So the measles virus of today has the same antigens as the measles virus of 1963, when the first vaccine was licensed. A flu virus's spikes can change shape and still work. Each year the flu viruses going round have drifted a little, and old antibodies fit less well. The World Health Organization studies flu samples from across the world and chooses the strains for the next vaccine twice a year. The common cold has a different problem. At least 165 types of rhinovirus are known, and antibodies against one type give little or no protection against the others. HIV is harder still. HIV changes faster than flu, and hides inside the very white blood cells that organise the defence. After forty years of work there is still no HIV vaccine.
examples: Measles: one kind of antigen that hardly changes. Two doses protect for many years.
Flu: antigens drift each year. A new vaccine is chosen twice a year, once for each half of the world.
Common cold: at least 165 types of rhinovirus. No vaccine exists.
explanations.art: Three rows of virus particles: the first row all identical, the second row each slightly different from the last, and the third row a crowd of many clearly different types.
explanations.context: This card explains why the measles vaccine lasts for years, why the flu vaccine changes every year, and why the common cold has no vaccine.

explanations.definition: A virus who can be copied only in human cells, and against whom a good vaccine exists, can be ended completely, because the virus needs an unbroken chain of human hosts.
explanations.description: A virus particle outside a cell does not last long. Every virus who infects only humans must keep reaching new humans, without a break, or that kind of virus ends. Smallpox infected only humans, and the vaccine was very good. After a worldwide effort, the last natural case was in Somalia in 1977, and the world was declared free of smallpox in 1980. Only one other disease has been ended in this way: rinderpest, a virus disease of cattle, whose end was announced in 2010. Polio may be the third. In the 1980s India had thousands of polio cases every year. The Pulse Polio programme began in 1995, with the aim of giving every child under five two drops of vaccine on the same days. India's last case of wild polio was recorded on 13 January 2011, in West Bengal. The World Health Organization declared India polio-free on 27 March 2014. Two of the three types of wild polio virus are now gone from the whole world. The third type still passes between people in Afghanistan and Pakistan. Until that chain breaks too, children everywhere still need the vaccine. A virus who also lives in other animals, such as rabies or bird flu, cannot be ended this way.
examples: Smallpox: only humans, a strong vaccine, eradicated in 1980.
Polio in India: Pulse Polio from 1995, the last wild case in January 2011, declared polio-free in March 2014.
Rabies: the virus also lives in dogs, bats and other animals, so vaccinating people alone cannot end it.
explanations.art: A health worker at a railway platform in India putting two drops into the mouth of a small child held by her mother, with a marker pen ready to mark the child's little finger.
explanations.context: This card explains why smallpox could be ended for good, how India ended wild polio, and why some viruses cannot be ended that way.

explanations.concept: Hidden viruses that stayed: virus DNA in our own genome
explanations.definition: Some viruses write their genome into the DNA of the host cell. When this happened long ago in an egg or sperm cell, the virus DNA was passed to the children. About 5 to 8 percent of human DNA came from such viruses.
explanations.description: Hiding in a cell's DNA can become permanent. A group of viruses called retroviruses make a DNA copy of their RNA genome and join it into the DNA of the host cell. HIV does this today. Usually the cell is a body cell, and the virus DNA ends when that person does. But over millions of years, retroviruses sometimes joined the DNA of an egg cell or a sperm cell. Then every cell of the child carried the virus DNA, and so did the child's children. When the human genome was read, scientists found that somewhere between 3 and 8 percent of it is made of these old virus genomes. Almost all of them are broken by mutations and can no longer make a virus. A few of their genes are still in use. One is called syncytin. In a retrovirus, the gene made the coat protein that fuses the virus with a cell. In us, the same protein fuses cells of the placenta into one continuous layer. That layer passes food from the mother to the baby and keeps the mother's defenders away from the baby. So a gene that once helped a virus enter cells now helps to build the organ that feeds a human baby before birth.
examples: HIV joins the DNA of white blood cells. That virus DNA is not inherited, because those cells are not egg or sperm cells.
The syncytin gene came from a retrovirus and is used in the human placenta.
Most of the old virus DNA in our genome is broken and makes nothing.
explanations.art: A long strand of DNA drawn as a ribbon with a few short sections shaded and labelled 'once a virus', and a small drawing of a baby joined to a placenta beside one of them.
explanations.context: This card explains how the genomes of ancient viruses came to be part of human DNA, and what one of their genes does in us today.

explanations.concept: Prions: a shape that gets copied
explanations.definition: A prion is a wrongly folded form of a normal body protein. When a prion touches a normal protein of the same kind, the normal one refolds into the prion shape. Prions have no DNA or RNA.
explanations.description: Your nerve cells carry a protein called PrP on their outer surface. Nobody is yet sure what it is for. In its normal shape the chain is folded mostly into coils. The same chain can also fold another way, into flat sheets that stack on top of each other. That second shape is the prion. The stacked form is very hard for the cell to break down. When a prion touches a normal PrP, the normal one changes to the stacked shape and joins the pile. The pile grows, breaks, and each piece grows again. No genome is copied. What passes on is a shape, and all the material comes from the cell's own normal protein. Mice that have no PrP gene cannot get prion disease at all, because there is nothing to convert. In the brain, the piles slowly damage nerve cells. Prion diseases take years to show and cannot yet be cured. They are also rare. Prions are much harder to destroy than viruses. Cooking does not destroy them, and hospitals need stronger methods than usual to clean instruments. In ordinary proteins a changed shape does not pass on. Cooked egg white does not cook the raw egg white beside it. A prion is unusual because its changed shape does.
examples: Kuru among the Fore people of Papua New Guinea, traced to funeral customs that ended around 1960.
Mad cow disease in Britain: more than 184,000 cattle were diagnosed between 1986 and 2015, after cattle were fed meal made from other cattle and sheep.
In Lemon, Chhena or Nothing, a piece of curdled milk did not curdle the fresh milk around it.
explanations.art: A row of neat coiled proteins on a cell surface, with a flat folded one at the left end touching its neighbour, which is half unwound and flattening.
explanations.context: This card explains what a prion is, and how a shape can be passed from one protein to the next without any genes.

explanations.description: All the prions known in humans and other mammals cause disease. In the early 1990s, Reed Wickner found that yeast cells have prions too. A yeast prion passes from a mother cell to her daughters in the cytoplasm, without any change in DNA. Yeast cells with a prion often behave differently from yeast cells without one. This raised a question that is still argued over. Is a prion always a protein gone wrong? Or can a cell use a shape that copies itself as a way to pass on a useful change?
examples: A yeast prion can change which sugars the cell can use, and the daughters inherit the change.
In mammals, no prion with a clear benefit has been shown.

perspectives.explanation: They argued that some yeast prions are useful. A prion can switch on hidden abilities, and in hard times a few cells with the prion may survive where the others do not.
They point out that prions are rare in wild yeast. If prions were useful they should be common, so most yeast prions are better seen as diseases of yeast.
They have proposed that prion-like proteins at the junctions between nerve cells help to keep long-term memories. This is an idea, tested mostly in sea slugs, fruit flies and mice, and not settled.

explanations.art: Two dishes of yeast colonies side by side, one white and one pink, with a small folded protein drawn above each.
explanations.context: This card is about a question scientists still argue over: whether a prion is always a harmful accident, or sometimes something a cell uses.

explanations.concept: Viroids: a bare loop of RNA
explanations.definition: A viroid is a closed loop of RNA, 246 to 467 letters long, with no protein coat. The loop holds no gene for any protein. Viroids are known only in plants, and a plant enzyme copies them.
explanations.description: In 1971, Theodor Diener, a plant scientist in Maryland in the United States, was studying a disease that makes potatoes long, thin and cracked. Everyone assumed that a virus caused it. But the thing that carried the disease was far too small to be any virus, and had no protein. It was a bare loop of RNA. He named it a viroid. A viroid's RNA is not a message for a ribosome, and no protein is ever made from it. So how are viroids copied? Inside the plant's nucleus there is an enzyme that copies DNA into mRNA. The viroid loop folds into a rod that this enzyme accepts, and the enzyme copies the loop round and round. The copies are cut and closed into new loops. Why the plant falls ill is only partly understood. Pieces of viroid RNA seem to match parts of the plant's own messages, and the plant's defences then cut up those messages too. Viroids move from plant to plant on cutting tools, by leaves touching, and through insects such as aphids. The best-known viroid is in coconut palms. The cadang-cadang viroid of the Philippines is only 246 letters long. A palm takes eight years or more to die. More than 30 million palms have died since the disease was first reported in the late 1920s, and it is spread mainly on the blades used for harvesting.
examples: Potato spindle tuber viroid, found by Theodor Diener in 1971, the first viroid known.
Coconut cadang-cadang viroid: 246 letters of RNA, and more than 30 million palms dead in the Philippines.
In the Knife Trail, turmeric from one piece of banana showed on several pieces that were cut afterwards with the same knife.
explanations.art: A coconut grove in which several palms have lost their crowns and stand as bare trunks, with a harvesting blade leaning against the nearest one.
explanations.context: This card explains what a viroid is, how a plant's own enzyme copies them, and how they killed millions of coconut palms.

explanations.description: Viroids are the smallest things known that are copied inside cells and cause disease. Nobody knows where they came from. The question matters because of an older question: what was there before cells? Many scientists think that before DNA and proteins, there was a time when RNA did both jobs, storing instructions and speeding up reactions. This is called the RNA world, and it is itself an idea, not a settled fact.
examples: Some viroids can cut themselves without any protein. RNA that speeds up a reaction is what the RNA world idea needs.
Viroids have so far been found only in plants, which appeared late in the history of life.

perspectives.explanation: He proposed that viroids are living relics of the RNA world: small loops of RNA that were being copied before there were any cells, and have carried on ever since.

They point out that viroids are found in plants and not in bacteria. Something left over from before cells should be in the oldest kinds of cell. They think viroids more likely escaped from the RNA of plant cells much later.
Recently, other small loops of RNA have been found in bacteria. Some researchers think this supports an old origin. The matter is open.

explanations.art: A timeline of life from four billion years ago to today with a small RNA loop drawn at the far left with a question mark, and another at the far right inside a potato plant.
explanations.context: This card is about an open question: whether viroids are left over from the time before cells, or escaped from plant cells later.

agreed.text: A virus particle builds nothing. The host cell's ribosomes build every virus protein, from messages that come from the virus genome.
agreed.evidence: Virus particles have no ribosomes, which can be seen under the electron microscope and in their list of genes. Virus proteins appear only in cells that still have working ribosomes.

agreed.text: After a virus enters a cell there is a stretch of time when no finished virus particle can be found in that cell.
agreed.evidence: Ellis and Delbrück counted phages in 1939 and found a flat stretch followed by a sudden jump. Later workers broke infected cells open early and found no whole particles inside.

agreed.text: Some viruses stay in a cell as a quiet genome for a long time, and can wake later.
agreed.evidence: Esther Lederberg showed in 1950 and 1951 that a strain of E. coli carried lambda phage through many generations without bursting. Shingles appears along one nerve decades after chickenpox, and the chickenpox virus is found in the blisters.

agreed.text: A vaccine protects by giving the body memory of an antigen before the real germ arrives.
agreed.evidence: Vaccinated people make antibodies within days of meeting the germ, where unvaccinated people take one to two weeks. Smallpox ended in 1980 and wild polio ended in India in 2011 after mass vaccination.

agreed.text: Prion diseases are passed on by a wrongly folded protein, with no DNA or RNA.
agreed.evidence: The scrapie agent survives doses of ultraviolet light and radiation that destroy DNA and RNA, as Tikvah Alper showed in 1967. Mice with no gene for the PrP protein cannot be infected.

agreed.text: Viroids are bare loops of RNA that hold no gene for any protein, and plant enzymes copy them.
agreed.evidence: Theodor Diener showed in 1971 that the cause of potato spindle tuber disease was RNA with no protein coat. The full sequences of viroids have been read, and no part of them is used to build a protein.

challenging.claim: Nothing can be copied and passed on unless it carries DNA or RNA.
challenging.who: Almost all biologists from the 1950s to the 1980s.
challenging.for: Every cell and every virus ever studied carried DNA or RNA, and the way those are copied was well understood.
challenging.against: Prions carry neither. The scrapie agent survives treatment that destroys DNA and RNA, and pure wrongly folded protein can pass the disease on. The rule holds for genes, but a shape can also be passed on.
challenging.context: This card is about an old rule of biology that prions showed to be too strict.

challenging.claim: A virus is a pure enemy of the living beings they infect.
challenging.who: The everyday view, and most of medicine until recently.
challenging.for: Viruses cause polio, measles, rabies, Covid and many diseases of crops and farm animals.
challenging.against: Most viruses infect bacteria and never harm a human. Phages kill a large share of the bacteria in the sea each day, which returns nutrients to the water. A gene that came from a virus builds part of the human placenta.
challenging.context: This card is about whether viruses are only harmful, or are also part of how the living world works.

challenging.claim: A vaccinated person cannot be infected at all.
challenging.for: For measles and smallpox, vaccinated people almost never fall ill.
challenging.against: A vaccine gives the body a head start. The virus may still enter some cells and be copied for a short time before antibodies stop the spread. For flu and Covid, vaccinated people are often infected and are ill for less time and less severely.
challenging.context: This card is about what a vaccine can and cannot do.

challenging.claim: An infected cell is not a damaged cell. It is the virus in their living form.
challenging.who: The French biologist Patrick Forterre, who calls the infected cell a 'virocell'.
challenging.for: Inside the cell, the virus genome directs feeding, building and copying. The particle outside is like a seed or a spore, a travelling stage.
challenging.against: All the machinery and energy still belong to the cell, and the cell has a genome of their own too. Most biologists prefer to say that there is one living cell, which is being used.
challenging.context: This card is about a view that changes what we mean by 'a virus': the particle, or the infected cell?

challenging.claim: Kuru was passed from parent to child in the genes.
challenging.for: Kuru ran in families and was found almost only among the Fore people.
challenging.against: It struck mostly women and children, which inherited diseases do not usually do. The anthropologists Shirley Lindenbaum and Robert Glasse traced it to funeral customs in which women and children took part most. In the 1960s Carleton Gajdusek's team passed kuru to a chimpanzee, which showed that it could be caught.
challenging.context: This card is about kuru, a prion disease of the Fore people of Papua New Guinea, and an early wrong explanation of it.

challenging.claim: Viroids are living relics from the time before cells.
challenging.who: Theodor Diener, who found the first viroid, in 1989.
challenging.for: Viroids are tiny loops of RNA, and some can cut themselves without proteins. That is what the earliest things to be copied are thought to have been like.
challenging.against: Viroids have been found only in plants, which appeared late. They may have escaped from the RNA of plant cells.
challenging.context: This card is about where viroids came from, which is not known.

big_questions.q: A cell's ribosomes build from any message with the right start. Would a cell be better off if they built only from the cell's own messages?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the cell would lose. How would it be vaccinated? How do new genes ever get used?
big_questions.context: This question comes from the Factory Test, in which you built whatever each grain said.

big_questions.q: The cell did all the building. The virus supplied only the instructions. So who made the new viruses?
big_questions.hint: Think of a cook who follows a recipe sent by a stranger. Who made the dish?
big_questions.context: This question is about how a virus is copied: the cell's ribosomes do the work, from the virus's messages.

big_questions.q: After chickenpox, the virus stays in your nerve cells for life. Are they now part of you, a guest, or neither?
big_questions.hint: Some virus DNA has been in the human genome for millions of years and builds part of the placenta. Does time change the answer?
big_questions.context: This question is about viruses who stay hidden in the body for many years.

big_questions.q: A prion passes on a shape and no genes. Is a shape a kind of information?
big_questions.hint: A footprint in wet cement can shape the next person's step. What gets passed on there?
big_questions.context: This question is about prions, which are wrongly folded proteins that make normal proteins fold wrongly too.

big_questions.q: Your vaccine protects you and also the baby next door who is too young for it. Is being vaccinated a choice about yourself or about everyone?
big_questions.hint: A virus needs an unbroken chain of hosts. What happens to the chain at each vaccinated person?
big_questions.context: This question is about vaccines, which stop a virus from being passed on as well as protecting one person.

big_questions.q: People ended smallpox on purpose. Is it right to end a whole kind of being for good?
big_questions.hint: Samples of smallpox virus are still kept frozen in two laboratories. People still argue about whether to destroy them.
big_questions.context: This question is about eradication, which means ending a disease everywhere in the world.

big_questions.q: For twenty years almost nobody would pay for Katalin Karikó's work. How should people decide which ideas are worth years of trying?
big_questions.hint: Her idea was right. Many ideas that nobody will pay for are wrong. How could anyone have told the difference in 1995?
big_questions.context: This question is about the scientist whose work on mRNA made the first mRNA vaccines possible.

story.title: The Stripe
story.note: Yazhini, her family, Dr Shahana and the summer of 1962 are made up. These facts are real. Shingles is caused by the chickenpox virus, who stays in nerve cells beside the spine for life after chickenpox. When the virus wakes, they travel along one nerve, so the rash forms a band on one side of the body and stops at the middle. About one person in three gets shingles at some time. The medicine works best if started within three days of the rash. A person cannot catch shingles from someone else, but someone who has never had chickenpox or the vaccine can catch chickenpox from the fluid in the blisters. In Tamil, shingles is commonly called akki.
text: For two days Paatti said that the left side of her back was burning, though nothing showed on the skin.
On the third morning Yazhini's mother lifted the edge of Paatti's blouse and drew in her breath. A band of small blisters ran from beside the spine, under the arm, and round to the front.
'Akki,' said the neighbour, who had come to return a steel dabba and stayed to look. 'My uncle had it. It goes away. But keep the baby from her.'
Yazhini was eleven, and she did not like answers that came without reasons. She looked at the band for a long time.

It was about as wide as her hand. It began at the middle of Paatti's back and ended at the middle of her chest. It did not cross either line by so much as one blister. The right side of Paatti was as smooth as ever.
'Who gave it to you?' Yazhini asked.
'Nobody,' said Paatti. 'I have not gone past the gate in two weeks, with this knee.'
'Somebody who came here, then.'
'The milk boy. The woman who brings greens. You. Which of you has akki?'

None of them had. Yazhini took her notebook to the back step and wrote down what she knew, the way her science teacher had shown her. One: it burned before it showed. Two: nobody brought it. Three: it kept to one side. Four: it stopped at the middle as if someone had ruled a line.

She thought about the things that give a rash from outside. A caterpillar. A new soap. The sap of the mango tree. But a caterpillar walks where they like. Soap goes everywhere the water goes. None of them would stop at the middle of a person.
So what is there in a body that stops at the middle?
Her brother's Class 9 biology book was on the shelf above the rice bin. She turned the pages until she found a picture of a person with no skin, only the nerves drawn in yellow.

The nerves came out from the spine in pairs, one to the left and one to the right, at every level from the neck down. Each one curved round its own side of the body like half a hoop on a barrel. Each one ended at the front, at the middle.

Yazhini put her finger on one yellow half-hoop on the left side, at about the height of the bottom of the ribs. She ran her finger along it, from the back to the front. Then she closed the book and went to look at Paatti again.
It was the same path.
At the government hospital that afternoon, Dr Shahana looked at the band for about four seconds and then asked a question that seemed to have nothing to do with it.
'Amma, did you have chickenpox when you were small?'

Paatti laughed. 'In Kumbakonam, the summer I was seven. Nineteen sixty-two. They kept me in the back room for two weeks with neem leaves on the bed. My sister Kamala was not allowed in, so she pushed slices of raw mango with salt under the door.'

'Then that is where this came from,' said the doctor. 'When the chickenpox ended, a few of the viruses did not leave. They went up the nerves and settled beside your spine, in the roots of the nerves. They have been quiet there ever since. Your body kept them quiet. Now you are seventy, and you have been tired and in pain with that knee. In one nerve root, they woke. They have come back down that one nerve to the skin.'
Yazhini stood very still. 'So it came from inside,' she said. 'Along one nerve. That is why it is a stripe.'
The doctor turned to look at her properly. 'Who told you that?'
'The stripe did. And my brother's book.'

'Then you have done half my work,' said Dr Shahana, and wrote out the tablets. 'These slow the virus down. It is good that you came on the third day, because they do the most when they are started early. The blisters will dry in a week or ten days. Until they have dried, keep them covered, and keep away anyone who has not had chickenpox or the vaccine. They cannot catch this from you. But they can catch chickenpox.'
Yazhini's mother found the old vaccination card in her handbag and showed it. Two doses, when Yazhini was small. The baby next door had had none yet. He would have to wave from the gate for a while.
On the bus home Paatti was quiet, and Yazhini did the subtraction on the back of the hospital slip. Two thousand and twenty-five take away nineteen sixty-two. Sixty-three years.
'Paatti,' she said, 'nobody gave it to you. You got it from a girl of seven in Kumbakonam.'
Paatti looked out at the paddy fields going past, flat and green to the edge of the sky.

'Kamala died eleven years ago,' she said after a while. 'I thought I had nothing left of that summer but the taste of the mango.' She put her hand lightly against her left side, over the cloth. 'And all this time it was travelling with me.'

That night Yazhini drew the person from the biology book in her own notebook, with every yellow half-hoop. She coloured one of them red, on the left, under the ribs. Under the drawing she wrote the four things she had known that morning, and then a fifth. Five: a virus can wait.
story.epiphany: The rash kept to one side and stopped at the middle of the body. Nothing that touches the skin from outside does that, but a nerve does. So the virus had come from inside, along one nerve. They had been in Paatti's body since she had chickenpox at seven. Entering a cell and bursting out at once is only one of the things a virus can do. A virus can also stay hidden for most of a lifetime.
ask: Yazhini decided the rash had not come from outside. Which of her four clues told her most? Why?
The virus was in Paatti's nerve cells for 63 years without making her ill. What do you think kept them quiet?
Why can the baby next door catch chickenpox from Paatti's blisters, but not shingles?
Paatti said the virus had been travelling with her all this time. Is a virus who stays for life a part of the person? What do you think?
art: A girl of eleven sitting on the back step of a tiled house in a Tamil Nadu town, writing a numbered list in a notebook, with a mango tree behind her.
An open biology textbook showing the outline of a human body with nerves drawn as yellow half-hoops curving from the spine round each side to the front, and a child's finger tracing one of them.
A grandmother in a cotton sari and her granddaughter side by side on a town bus, the grandmother looking out at green paddy fields with her hand resting against her left side.

games.title: Seven Steps or Stopped: a virus against a body, with and without a vaccine
games.context: This is a card and dice game about the seven steps a virus goes through in a cell. One player is the virus and one is the body. You play it once for a body with no vaccine and once for a body with a vaccine, and compare.

printables.title: 7 step cards to cut out (what happens is on the back)

items.b: A spike on the virus's coat fits a receptor on the cell, and the two stick together.
The cell takes the virus in, or the virus's envelope joins with the cell's membrane.
The coat comes apart and the genome is free inside the cell. No whole virus exists in the cell now.
The cell's ribosomes build virus proteins from the virus's messages.
The virus genome is copied many times, using the cell's materials.
New coat proteins and new genomes come together as new virus particles.
The new particles burst the cell, or bud out through the cell's membrane.

printables.title: 13 defence cards to cut out (how it works is on the back)

items.b: Antibodies cover the virus's spikes, so the spikes no longer fit the receptor.
Antibodies cover the virus's spikes, so the spikes no longer fit the receptor.
Sticky mucus in the nose and throat traps virus particles before they reach a cell.
Some medicines for HIV stop the virus's envelope from joining with the cell's membrane.
One older flu medicine works by stopping the flu virus's coat from coming apart inside the cell.
A warned cell slows their ribosomes, so few virus proteins are built.
A warned cell slows their ribosomes, so few virus proteins are built.
A warned cell makes an enzyme that cuts up RNA, including the virus's.
The medicine given for shingles stops the chickenpox virus's DNA from being copied.
A badly infected cell self-destructs before the new particles are finished.
Some medicines for HIV stop the virus's proteins from being cut to the right size, so no finished particle forms.
A white blood cell finds the infected cell and destroys that cell before the new particles get out.
One flu medicine stops new flu particles from breaking free of the cell's surface.

rules: You need the 7 step cards, the 13 defence cards, 5 groundnuts and a die. The groundnuts are virus particles.
One player is the Virus and one is the Body. Alone, you play the Body, and the virus moves by the rules.
Lay the 7 step cards in a row, from ATTACH to LEAVE. Shuffle the defence cards into a pile, face down. In the first game the Body starts with no cards.
The Virus puts one groundnut on ATTACH. Each time a groundnut is put on ATTACH, the Body draws one card. Each time a groundnut reaches READ, the Body draws one more card.

If the Body holds a card that names the step the groundnut is on, the Body may play it. Then roll the die. On 3, 4, 5 or 6 the particle is stopped, and the groundnut is taken away. On 1 or 2 the virus slips past. The card is used up either way.
Only one card may be played on each step. If the groundnut is not stopped, it moves to the next step.
When a groundnut is stopped, the Virus starts the next one on ATTACH. If the pile runs out, the Body plays on with the cards in hand.
The Virus wins if one groundnut gets past LEAVE. The Body wins if all 5 groundnuts are stopped.
Second game, with a vaccine: before shuffling, the Body takes the two ANTIBODY cards into their hand. Everything else is the same. Play each game three times and count who wins.

setup.caption: 2. The Body plays a card that names the step the groundnut is on.

setup.art: A die showing 5 beside the row of step cards, and a hand lifting the groundnut off the row.
setup.caption: 3. Roll. On 3 to 6 the particle is stopped. On 1 or 2 the virus slips past.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Lay the step cards in order and read each back aloud. 3. Shuffle the defence cards. 4. Decide who is the Virus and who is the Body. 5. Ask for a guess: who will win more often with no vaccine?
flow.say: A virus particle has to get through seven steps. The body has defences, but it starts with none in hand. Who do you think will win more often? Why?
flow.kid: Lay the 7 step cards in order. Read the backs. Shuffle the defence cards. Guess who wins more often with no vaccine. Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of Seven Steps or Stopped. Here you set out the seven step cards and guess whether the virus or the body wins more often.

flow.do: 1. Play three games with no vaccine. 2. The Body draws one card when a groundnut starts, and one more when a groundnut reaches READ. 3. After each game, mark V or B on the tally sheet.
flow.say: The body draws its second card only when the virus reaches READ. Why might that be a fair rule?
flow.kid: Play three games with no vaccine. Draw one card when a groundnut starts. Draw one more when a groundnut reaches READ. Mark who wins each game.

ask.q: Why does the body get a card when the virus reaches READ?
good: That is when the cell senses virus messages and raises the alarm.
The body cannot respond to a virus it has not noticed yet.

flow.parent: With no vaccine the Virus wins roughly half the games. The first particle often gets through, because the Body has so few cards early on.
flow.context: In this step of Seven Steps or Stopped you play three games in which the body has no vaccine and starts with no defence cards.

flow.do: 1. Find the two ANTIBODY cards and give them to the Body. 2. Shuffle the other 11 cards. 3. Play three games in the same way. 4. Mark V or B on the tally sheet.
flow.say: This body has had a vaccine. It starts with two antibody cards. What do you think will change? Why?
flow.kid: Give the Body the two ANTIBODY cards first. Shuffle the rest. Play three more games. Mark who wins each one.
flow.parent: With the two antibody cards the Body wins most games. The Virus still wins now and then, on a roll of 1 or 2. A vaccine gives a head start and is not a wall.
flow.context: In this step of Seven Steps or Stopped you play three games in which the body has had a vaccine and starts with two antibody cards.

flow.do: 1. Count the wins on each side of the tally sheet. 2. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Look at the two columns. What did the vaccine change? Did it ever fail?
flow.kid: Count the wins in each column. What did the vaccine change? Did the virus ever win against it?

ask.q: The vaccine cards stop only one step. Why does that help so much?
good: They stop the very first step, before the virus is inside a cell.
The body has them ready at the start.

ask.q: A roll of 1 or 2 lets the virus past a defence. What might that stand for in real life?
good: A virus whose coat has changed a little.
Too many virus particles for the antibodies to cover.
Chance.

check.q: What does a vaccine give the body in this game?
options: Defence cards in hand before the virus arrives
check.why: A vaccinated body holds antibody cards from the start, as a real body holds memory cells and antibodies. The virus's steps do not change. If you chose 'fewer steps', remember that the virus still has all seven to get through.

flow.parent: Three games each is a small number, so one family may see the Virus win twice with a vaccine. Add your results to another day's and the pattern becomes clear.
flow.context: This is the last step of Seven Steps or Stopped. Here you compare the games with and without a vaccine and say what the vaccine changed.

games.title: Who Am I? Virus, prion, viroid or bacterium
games.context: This is a clue card game about four kinds of very small things: a virus, a prion, a viroid and a bacterium. Each card gives one clue, and you say which of the four it fits.

printables.title: 20 clue cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: I have a protein coat around my genome, and no ribosomes.
items.b: VIRUS. A virus particle is a genome in a protein coat. Some have a fatty envelope too.

items.f: I am one protein, folded the wrong way. I have no genes at all.
items.b: PRION. A prion has the same chain as a normal body protein, in a different shape.

items.f: I am a bare loop of RNA with no coat.
items.b: VIROID. A viroid is 246 to 467 letters of RNA and nothing else.

items.f: I have my own ribosomes and can multiply in a bowl of warm milk.
items.b: BACTERIUM. A bacterium is a whole cell and builds their own proteins.

items.f: A plant enzyme copies me. No protein is ever made from me.
items.b: VIROID. The plant's own RNA-making enzyme copies the loop.
BACTERIUM. Antibiotics act on parts that bacteria have. They do nothing to a virus, a prion or a viroid.

items.f: A vaccine can get the body ready for me.
items.b: VIRUS or BACTERIUM. There are vaccines against measles and polio viruses, and against tetanus and typhoid bacteria.
PRION. Prions survive cooking, and hospitals need extra-strong cleaning to remove them.

items.f: I have killed more than 30 million coconut palms.
items.b: VIROID. The cadang-cadang viroid of the Philippines.

items.f: I can stay hidden in a nerve cell for sixty years.
items.b: VIRUS. The chickenpox virus stays in nerve cells for life and can wake as shingles.

items.f: A cell's ribosomes build my parts from my messages.
items.b: VIRUS. A viroid is copied by an enzyme, but no ribosome ever reads a viroid.

items.f: What I pass on is a shape.
items.b: PRION. A prion makes normal proteins of the same kind refold into the prion shape.

items.f: Ultraviolet light that wrecks DNA and RNA does not stop me.
items.b: PRION. This is how Tikvah Alper showed in 1967 that the scrapie agent had no DNA or RNA.

items.f: I split in two, and can do it every 20 minutes when I am well fed.
items.b: BACTERIUM. E. coli in a warm, rich broth can divide about every 20 minutes.

items.f: I have been found only in plants.
items.b: VIROID. No viroid has been found in any animal.

items.f: I store pieces of my attackers' DNA and pass that record to my daughters.
items.b: BACTERIUM. The record is called CRISPR.

items.f: Soap pulls apart my fatty envelope.
items.b: VIRUS. Flu and Covid viruses have a fatty envelope taken from the cell they budded from.

items.f: I travel from plant to plant on knives and harvesting blades.
items.b: VIROID. Some plant viruses travel this way too, so VIRUS is also a fair answer.

items.f: A mouse with no gene for the protein I am made of can never catch me.
items.b: PRION. With no normal protein to refold, a prion has nothing to work on.

items.f: I can write my genome into the DNA of my host.
items.b: VIRUS. HIV does this in white blood cells, and lambda phage does it in bacteria.

rules: Shuffle the 20 cards and put them in a pile with the clues facing up.
On your turn, read the top clue aloud. Say which it fits: virus, prion, viroid or bacterium.
Turn the card over. If you were right, keep the card. If not, put it at the bottom of the pile.
A few clues fit two answers. The back says so. Either answer wins the card.
The game ends when the pile is gone. The player with the most cards wins.
Alone: go through the pile once and count how many you got right the first time. Play again tomorrow and try to beat your score.

setup.art: A pile of small cards with a line of writing on the top one, and four paper labels beside it reading Virus, Prion, Viroid and Bacterium.
setup.caption: 1. Shuffle the 20 clue cards into a pile, clues up.

setup.art: A child reading a card aloud and pointing to the label 'Prion', while a second player waits.
setup.caption: 2. Read the clue. Say which of the four it fits.

setup.art: A hand turning a card over to show the answer on its back.
setup.caption: 3. Turn it over. If you were right, keep the card.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 20 cards. 2. Write the four names on slips: virus, prion, viroid, bacterium. 3. Ask your child to say one fact about each before you start.
flow.say: Four very small things. Tell me one fact about each that you remember.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Write the four names on slips. Say one fact you remember about each.
flow.context: This is the first step of Who Am I? Here you set out the clue cards and say one fact each about a virus, a prion, a viroid and a bacterium.

flow.do: 1. Play by the rules. 2. After each card, read the back aloud. 3. Keep going until the pile is gone.
flow.say: Read the clue aloud. Which of the four is it? Tell me how you know.
flow.kid: Read the top clue. Say which of the four it fits. Turn it over. Keep it if you were right.
flow.parent: The clues about copying are the hardest. A ribosome reads a virus's messages, but nothing reads a viroid. An enzyme only copies the loop.
flow.context: In this step of Who Am I? you take turns reading a clue and saying whether it fits a virus, a prion, a viroid or a bacterium.

flow.do: 1. Count the cards each player holds. 2. Lay out the cards that were missed the first time. 3. Ask which clue was hardest, and why.
flow.say: Which clue was hardest? What would you need to know to get it right next time?
flow.kid: Count your cards. Look at the ones you missed. Which clue was hardest? Why?

check.q: Which of the four has no DNA and no RNA?
check.why: A prion is only protein. A viroid is nothing but RNA, a virus has DNA or RNA inside a coat, and a bacterium has both. If you chose a viroid, you remembered 'the one with least', but a viroid's whole body is RNA.

flow.context: This is the last step of Who Am I? Here you count your cards and look again at the clues you missed.

experiments.title: The Factory Test: whose jobs get done inside an infected cell?
experiments.context: In this experiment a steel tumbler is a model cell. Plain grains are the cell's own messages and marked grains are a virus's messages. You draw six grains each round and count whose jobs get done.
experiments.question: One virus message gets into a cell that holds twenty messages of their own. The virus message is copied each round. After how many rounds is half of the cell's work being done for the virus?
experiments.predict: Guess first. You will draw 6 grains in each of 7 rounds. In which round will 3 or more of the 6 be marked grains for the first time? Will the number of marked grains you draw rise evenly, or slowly at first and then fast? Why do you think so? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: Every round uses the same tumbler, the same shake and six draws with eyes shut. Only the number of marked grains changes, and it doubles each round. In the second run only one thing is changed: the cell starts with 40 plain grains in place of 20.

materials.item: white chana, groundnuts or any pale grain that a pen can mark
a sketch pen or marker
a steel tumbler or a small dabba that you cannot see into from the side
a small bowl
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Set up a model cell with 20 plain grains and 1 marked grain. Run 7 rounds of drawing and copying. Then run it again with 40 plain grains and compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for all 7 rounds of each run. Draw a line graph of the virus jobs out of 6 against the round number, one line for each run. Then write one sentence each for what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results from one run with 20 plain grains
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a filled table can look like. Your draws will be different, because chance decides which grains you pick.

setup.art: A steel tumbler holding twenty pale chana and one chana with a dark pen mark, beside a small bowl heaped with more pale chana and a sketch pen.
setup.caption: 1. Put 20 plain grains and 1 marked grain in the tumbler. Put 70 plain grains in the bowl.

setup.art: A child with eyes shut lifting one grain out of a steel tumbler, with five grains already in a row on the table, one of them marked.
setup.caption: 2. Shake. With eyes shut, draw 6 grains one at a time. Count the marked ones.

setup.art: A child marking pale chana from the bowl with a sketch pen and dropping them into the tumbler.
setup.caption: 3. Put the 6 back. For every marked grain in the tumbler, mark one more from the bowl and add it.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a table of seven rows, the last column of numbers getting larger towards the bottom.
setup.caption: 4. Write each round in the table. Do 7 rounds.

flow.do: 1. Count 20 plain grains into the tumbler. 2. Mark one more grain with the pen and add it. 3. Put 70 plain grains in the bowl. 4. Draw the table with five columns and seven rows. 5. Read the question aloud and ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: The tumbler is a cell. Each plain grain is one of the cell's own messages. The marked grain is a message from a virus who has just got in. Each round you are the cell's builder. You pick six messages without looking and build whatever they say. In which round will half of your six be for the virus? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put 20 plain grains and 1 marked grain in the tumbler. Put 70 plain grains in the bowl. Draw the table. Guess the round when 3 of your 6 are marked. Write why.
flow.parent: Many children guess round 2 or 3, and expect an even rise. Write the guess down and do not correct it. The bowl is the cell's store of building materials.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Factory Test. Here you set up a tumbler as a model cell and guess when a virus's messages will take most of the work.

flow.do: 1. Shake the tumbler. 2. Your child shuts their eyes and draws 6 grains, one at a time. 3. Count the marked and the plain ones and write them in the table. 4. Put all 6 back. 5. Now the virus message is copied. For every marked grain in the tumbler, mark one grain from the bowl and add it. 6. Do rounds 1, 2, 3 and 4 in this way.
flow.say: Take the first grain your fingers touch. Do not feel for a mark. After each round, every virus message gets one copy. The copies are made from the cell's own store.
flow.kid: Shake. Shut your eyes. Draw 6 grains, one at a time. Count the marked ones. Put them back. Then mark one new grain for every marked grain in the tumbler. Do 4 rounds.

ask.q: After round 3, how many marked grains are in the tumbler? How do you know without counting them?
good: Four. It went 1, then 2, then 4.
It doubles each round.

flow.parent: The marked grains in the tumbler go 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64. In rounds 1 to 3 most children draw no marked grain or just one. Let your child notice this without comment.
flow.context: In this step of the Factory Test you run the first four rounds. Each round you draw six grains from the model cell and then copy every marked grain.

flow.do: 1. Do rounds 5, 6 and 7 in the same way. 2. After round 7, do not copy again. 3. Look at the bowl and count what is left in it.
flow.say: Keep going for three more rounds. Watch what happens to the store in the bowl.
flow.kid: Do rounds 5, 6 and 7. Stop after round 7. Count the grains left in the bowl.

ask.q: What happened to the cell's store of materials?
good: It is nearly used up.
Only 7 grains are left out of 70.
The virus copies were made from the cell's own store.

flow.parent: Most runs first reach 3 or more marked grains in round 5. Round 4 or round 6 is also common, because chance decides each draw. The bowl should hold 7 grains at the end.
flow.context: In this step of the Factory Test you run rounds 5 to 7 of the model cell, and see what is left of the cell's store of materials.

flow.do: 1. Look at the filled table together. 2. Ask what your child notices. 3. Ask the questions below. 4. Do not explain yet.
flow.say: Look down the column of virus jobs. What do you notice? Did anything force you to build for the virus?
flow.kid: Look down the column of virus jobs. What do you notice? Say it out loud. Did anyone force you to pick marked grains?

ask.q: In rounds 1 to 3 you drew almost no marked grains. Was the virus in the cell during those rounds?
good: Yes, from the start.
They were there and doubling, but there were too few to be picked often.

ask.q: Why did you build more and more for the virus?
good: There were more and more marked grains, so I picked them more often.
I built whatever I picked. I did not check whose it was.

ask.q: What happened to the cell's own jobs?
good: Fewer and fewer got done.
By round 7 only one or two of the six were for the cell.

check.q: During which rounds was the virus message inside the model cell?
options: Only in rounds when you drew a marked grain
check.why: The marked grain was in the tumbler from round 1 and doubled every round. In the early rounds there were too few to be drawn often. If you chose rounds 6 and 7, you were thinking of when the virus showed. A real infection also has a quiet time before anything shows.

flow.parent: Good answers mention the quiet early rounds, the fast rise at the end, and that nothing was forced. If your child's run was unusual, say so and keep the numbers. Chance is part of the model.
flow.context: In this step of the Factory Test you look at your table of seven rounds and say what you notice about whose jobs got done.

flow.do: 1. Empty the tumbler. Keep the 64 marked grains in one pile. 2. Put 40 plain grains and 1 marked grain in the tumbler. 3. Ask for a new guess and a reason. 4. Run 7 rounds as before. To copy, add marked grains from the pile. 5. Fill in a second table.
flow.say: This cell is twice as busy. It has 40 messages of its own. Will the virus take much longer to get half of your 6 jobs? How many rounds longer? Why do you think so?
