flow.kid: Start again with 40 plain grains and 1 marked grain. Guess how much longer the virus will take. Write why. Run 7 rounds. Add marked grains from your pile to copy.
flow.parent: Many children guess that it will take twice as long. It usually takes just one round longer, and sometimes no longer at all. About one run in twenty does not get there in 7 rounds. Doubling catches up very fast.
flow.context: In this step of the Factory Test you run the model cell again with 40 plain grains in place of 20, to see how much a busier cell slows the virus.

flow.do: 1. Put the two tables side by side. 2. Ask what the model shows, and what it leaves out. 3. Your child writes three sentences: what I thought, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: A real cell has millions of builders called ribosomes, and many thousands of messages. Our tumbler had six draws and twenty messages. What did the model get right? What did it leave out?
flow.kid: Compare the two tables. What did the model get right? What did it leave out? Write what you thought, what you saw, and why.

ask.q: What does the model leave out?
good: A real cell has far more messages and builders.
The cell fights back, and our model cell did not.
Some viruses also destroy the cell's messages.

flow.parent: Now you can explain. A ribosome builds from whichever message it meets. More virus messages means more virus jobs. The model leaves out the cell's defences and the tricks of real viruses.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Factory Test. Here you compare your two runs of the model cell and say what the model shows and what it leaves out.

experiments.title: Lemon, Chhena or Nothing: can changed milk change fresh milk?
experiments.safety: A grown-up heats the milk and pours it. Hot milk scalds.
experiments.context: In this experiment you curdle a little milk with lemon juice. Then you test whether a piece of the curdled milk can curdle fresh milk. It helps to show why a prion is so unusual.
experiments.question: Lemon juice changes the protein in milk into solid lumps. Can a lump of that changed protein make fresh milk change too?
experiments.predict: Guess first. You will drop a rinsed lump of curdled milk into a tumbler of hot fresh milk. After 10 minutes, will the fresh milk have curdled, partly curdled, or stayed the same? Why do you think so? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: All three tumblers get the same milk, the same amount, the same heat and the same wait. Only what is added changes: lemon juice in A, a rinsed lump of curdled milk in B, and nothing in C.

materials.item: milk
materials.qty: 300 millilitres, about one and a half tea glasses

materials.item: a lemon, or 2 teaspoons of vinegar
small steel tumblers or glasses
a tea strainer and a teaspoon
a small pan, and a stove

schedule.what: Curdle a little hot milk with lemon juice. Rinse a lump of it. Drop the lump into fresh hot milk and watch for 10 minutes beside a tumbler of plain milk.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for tumblers A, B and C. Draw each tumbler as it looked after 10 minutes. Then write one sentence each for what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

setup.art: A grown-up pouring hot milk from a small pan into a steel tumbler marked A, with half a lemon and a teaspoon beside it.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up heats the milk. Pour a third into tumbler A and add 2 teaspoons of lemon juice.

setup.art: A tea strainer held under a thin stream of tap water, with soft white lumps of curdled milk in it.
setup.caption: 2. Strain the lumps from A. Rinse them well under the tap to wash off the lemon.

setup.art: Three steel tumblers in a row labelled A, B and C: A holding thin greenish liquid, B holding milk with one white lump being dropped in, and C holding plain milk.
setup.caption: 3. Pour hot milk into B and C. Drop one rinsed lump into B. Add nothing to C.

setup.art: A child looking closely into two tumblers of milk with a spoon in one hand, a clock on the wall behind.
setup.caption: 4. Wait 10 minutes. Stir B gently once. Compare B with C.

flow.do: 1. Label the tumblers A, B and C. 2. A grown-up heats the milk until it just begins to rise, then turns off the stove. 3. The grown-up pours one third of the milk into A. 4. Add 2 teaspoons of lemon juice to A and stir once. 5. Watch A for 2 minutes. 6. Put a lid on the pan to keep the rest hot.
flow.say: Watch tumbler A closely. Tell me what you see happening to the milk.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to heat the milk and pour some into A. Add 2 teaspoons of lemon juice. Stir once. Watch for 2 minutes. What happens?

ask.q: What has the milk in A turned into?
good: White lumps and a thin, pale liquid.
It has separated into solid bits and watery stuff.

flow.parent: Within a minute or two the milk separates into soft white lumps and a thin, pale greenish liquid. If it does not, the milk was not hot enough. Add one more teaspoon of lemon juice.
flow.context: This is the first step of Lemon, Chhena or Nothing. Here a grown-up heats milk, and you curdle a little of it with lemon juice.

flow.do: 1. Pour A through the tea strainer over the sink. 2. Hold the strainer under a slow tap for 30 seconds, and turn the lumps with the spoon. 3. Press out the water. 4. Read the question aloud and ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: These lumps are chhena, the solid that paneer is made from. The milk protein in them has changed. We have washed the lemon off. If we drop one lump into fresh hot milk, what will happen to that milk? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Strain the lumps. Rinse them under the tap for 30 seconds. Press out the water. Now guess. Will a lump change fresh milk? Write why.
flow.parent: Rinsing matters. Any lemon juice left on the lump would spoil the test. Many children guess that the lump will curdle the new milk, as a spoon of curd sets milk. Write the guess down and do not correct it.
flow.context: In this step of Lemon, Chhena or Nothing you rinse the lumps of curdled milk and guess whether one lump can curdle fresh milk.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up warms the rest of the milk again until it steams. 2. The grown-up pours half into B and half into C. 3. Drop one lump of rinsed chhena, about the size of a marble, into B. 4. Add nothing to C. 5. Note the time.
flow.say: B gets the lump. C gets nothing. Why do we need tumbler C at all?
flow.kid: A grown-up pours hot milk into B and C. Drop one lump into B. Add nothing to C. Note the time. Why do we need C?

ask.q: Why do we need tumbler C?
good: To see what hot milk does by itself.
So we know any change in B came from the lump.

flow.parent: C is the control. A skin may form on top of both B and C as they cool. That is normal for hot milk and is not curdling.
flow.context: In this step of Lemon, Chhena or Nothing you set up the test. One tumbler of hot milk gets a rinsed lump of curdled milk and one gets nothing.

flow.do: 1. Look at B and C after 2 minutes and write what you see. 2. After 5 minutes, stir B gently once. 3. After 10 minutes, look again. Lift a spoonful from each and compare. 4. Fill in the table.
flow.say: Look for lumps, for thin watery liquid, or for any change at all. Compare B with C each time.
flow.kid: Look at B and C after 2 minutes. Stir B once after 5 minutes. Look again after 10 minutes. Lift a spoonful from each. Fill in the table.

ask.q: What happened to the milk in B?
good: Nothing. It is still smooth milk, with the lump sitting in it.
It looks the same as C.

ask.q: What did change the milk in tumbler A?
good: The lemon juice.
The acid in the lemon.

flow.parent: B should stay smooth milk with the lump in it, the same as C. If B has curdled a little, some lemon was left on the lump. Rinse another lump for longer and try again. That result still tells you something: the lemon did it, and the lump did not.
flow.context: In this step of Lemon, Chhena or Nothing you watch two tumblers of hot milk for 10 minutes. One has a lump of curdled milk in it and one has nothing.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child what they think now, and what they saw. 2. Then read the note below together. 3. Your child writes three sentences: what I thought, what I saw, and why. 4. The milk in B and C is good to drink or to use for tea.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you see that tells you so?
flow.kid: Say what you think now. Say what you saw. Then write three sentences: what I thought, what I saw, and why.

check.q: A spoon of curd sets a pot of milk overnight. A lump of chhena does not. Why?
options: Curd is more sour than chhena
Chhena is too solid to mix in
Curd holds living bacteria who multiply
check.why: Curd carries living bacteria. They multiply in the milk and make acid, and the acid sets the milk. Rinsed chhena carries only changed milk protein, and that does not pass its change on. If you chose 'more sour', you were close: acid does the setting, but only the bacteria can keep making more of it.

flow.parent: Now you can explain. Acid from the lemon made the milk protein, called casein, tangle into lumps. The lumps do not make other casein tangle. In almost every protein, a changed form does not pass its change on. A prion is the rare protein whose changed form does. No kitchen test can show a prion at work, so this test shows what a prion is not. If your family eats eggs, try a piece of boiled egg white in raw egg white. The raw egg white stays raw.
flow.context: This is the last step of Lemon, Chhena or Nothing. Here you say what the test showed about whether a changed protein can change the protein beside it.

activities.title: Whose Note Is It? Do people follow a message without asking who sent it?
activities.context: In this activity you hand someone a short list of small jobs with no name on it, and watch what they do. It is a way into the question of how a virus takes over a cell.

materials.item: a slip of paper and a pen
a family member who has not seen this page

schedule.what: Write an unsigned list of five small jobs. Hand it to a family member and watch. Then list the written instructions you followed today.

activities.record: Write down which of the five jobs were done, and whether the person asked who wrote the list or why. Then write three written instructions that you yourself followed today without knowing who wrote them.

setup.art: A child writing a numbered list of five short lines on a small slip of paper, with no name at the top.
setup.caption: 1. Write five small, harmless jobs on a slip. Put no name on it.

setup.art: A grown-up reading a slip of paper in one hand and placing a spoon on a windowsill with the other, while a child watches from the doorway.
setup.caption: 2. Hand it to someone and say only: 'Could you do these, please?' Watch.

setup.art: A door with a 'Push' sign, a medicine bottle with 'Shake well' on the label, and a phone showing a forwarded message.
setup.caption: 3. Afterwards, list three written instructions you followed today without knowing who wrote them.

flow.do: 1. Your child writes five small jobs on a slip, with no name and no reason. 2. Four are ordinary, such as 'Bring one steel tumbler' and 'Fold one towel'. 3. One is harmless but odd, such as 'Put one spoon on the windowsill'. 4. Your child guesses what the person will do.
flow.say: Write five small jobs for someone at home. Make one of them a little odd, but harmless. Put no name on the slip. Do you think they will do all five? Will they ask who wrote it?
flow.kid: Write five small jobs on a slip. Make one a little odd, but harmless. Put no name on it. Guess: will the person do all five?
flow.parent: If only the two of you are at home, your child can test you. Do not read the rest of this activity first. If nobody is free, go straight to step 3.
flow.context: This is the first step of Whose Note Is It? Here you write an unsigned list of five small jobs for a family member.

flow.do: 1. Your child hands over the slip and says only, 'Could you do these, please?' 2. Your child watches without speaking. 3. Note which jobs are done, and any question the person asks.
flow.say: Hand it over and say only, 'Could you do these, please?' Then watch quietly. Notice what they do at the odd line.
flow.kid: Hand over the slip. Say only, 'Could you do these, please?' Watch quietly. Which jobs do they do? Do they ask anything?
flow.parent: Most people do all five, sometimes with a puzzled look at the odd line. Some ask why. Both results are worth writing down.
flow.context: In this step of Whose Note Is It? you hand someone an unsigned list of jobs and watch whether they do every job on it.

flow.do: 1. Tell the person it was a test, and thank them. 2. Ask why they did the odd job, or why they did not. 3. Together, list three written instructions each of you followed today without knowing who wrote them.
flow.say: Why did you do the odd one? Now let us each think of three written instructions we followed today. Who wrote each one?
flow.kid: Tell them it was a test. Ask why they did the odd job. Then list three written instructions you followed today. Who wrote each one?

ask.q: When is it sensible to follow a message without knowing who sent it?
good: When it is harmless or clearly useful, like 'Push' on a door.
When checking every message would take too long.

flow.think: A cell follows written instructions all day long. What might happen if a stranger's instruction got in among them?
flow.parent: Signs, labels, recipes and forwarded messages are good finds. Do not explain the link to viruses yet. The Factory Test comes next, and it will raise the question again.
flow.context: This is the last step of Whose Note Is It? Here you talk about why people follow written instructions without knowing who wrote them.

activities.title: Drift Cards: how much can a pattern change before you stop knowing it?
activities.context: In this activity you make six cards with a pattern that changes one square at a time. Then you test at which card a person stops recognising the pattern they learned. It is a model of why the flu vaccine is changed every year.

materials.item: paper cut into 6 squares, each about 6 centimetres wide
a pencil and a ruler
one or two family members to test

schedule.what: Make six cards with a 3 by 3 pattern that changes by one square each time. Test at which card a person says the pattern is new.

activities.record: Make a table with two columns: the number of changed squares, and what the person said (same, not sure or different). Under it, write the number of changes at which they first said 'different'.

setup.art: A square paper card with a 3 by 3 grid, four of the nine squares shaded with pencil, and the number 0 on the back corner.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a 3 by 3 grid on a card. Shade any 4 squares. This is card 0.

setup.art: Six cards in a row, each with a 3 by 3 grid, each pattern differing from the one before by a single square.
setup.caption: 2. Make cards 1 to 5. Each one copies the card before, with one more square changed.

setup.art: A child holding up one pattern card to a grown-up who is looking at it, with the other cards face down on the table.
setup.caption: 3. Show card 0 for 10 seconds. Hide it. Then show the others one at a time and ask: same or different?

flow.do: 1. Draw a 3 by 3 grid on each of the 6 cards. 2. On card 0, shade any 4 squares. Write 0 on the back. 3. On card 1, copy card 0 and then change one square: shade an empty one, or leave a shaded one empty. 4. On card 2, copy card 1 and change one more square, a different one. 5. Go on to card 5. Number the backs.
flow.say: Card 0 is the coat of a virus this year. Each new card is the same virus one year later, with one small copying change.
flow.kid: Draw a 3 by 3 grid on each card. Shade 4 squares on card 0. Each next card copies the last one, with one square changed. Number the backs 0 to 5.
flow.parent: Check that each card changes a square that has not been changed before. Card 5 then differs from card 0 in five squares.
flow.context: This is the first step of Drift Cards. Here you make six pattern cards, each one square different from the card before.

flow.do: 1. Explain the test. A person will study card 0 for 10 seconds. Then they will see the cards one at a time for 3 seconds each. 2. Ask your child to guess at which card the person will first say 'different', and why.
flow.say: The person is the body. They learn the pattern on card 0, as the body learns a virus's coat from a vaccine. At which card will they first say it is a different pattern? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A person will learn card 0. Then they see the other cards. Guess: at which card will they first say 'different'? Write why.
flow.parent: Any guess with a reason is good. Many children expect card 1 to be spotted at once.
flow.context: In this step of Drift Cards you guess how many squares must change before a person stops recognising the pattern they learned.

flow.do: 1. Show the person card 0 for a slow count of 10. Then hide it. 2. Shuffle cards 0 to 5. 3. Show each card for a count of 3 and ask, 'Same as the one you learned, different, or not sure?' 4. Write each answer beside the card's number. 5. If there is time, test a second person.
flow.say: Look at this pattern for ten seconds. Now I will show you six cards. For each one, tell me: same, different or not sure.
flow.kid: Show card 0 for 10 seconds. Hide it. Shuffle all six cards. Show each for 3 seconds. Ask: same, different or not sure? Write down each answer.
flow.parent: Most people call cards 0 and 1 the same, are unsure at 2 or 3, and say 'different' by 4 or 5. People vary, and that is part of the finding.
flow.context: In this step of Drift Cards you test a family member. They learn one pattern, and then say whether each changed card is the same or different.

flow.do: 1. Put the cards in order from 0 to 5 with the answers beside them. 2. Ask what your child notices. 3. Then talk about the flu vaccine.
flow.say: Look at the answers in order. Did the person stop recognising the pattern all at once, or bit by bit? What does that tell you about a virus whose coat changes a little each year?
flow.kid: Put the cards in order. Look at the answers. Did the person stop knowing the pattern all at once, or bit by bit?

ask.q: After one changed square, did the person still know the pattern?
good: Yes, mostly.
A small change was still close enough.

ask.q: Why might last year's flu vaccine protect a little this year, but not well?
good: The coat has drifted a bit, so the old antibodies still fit partly.
After enough changes they no longer fit.

flow.parent: Antibodies fit by shape, so a slightly changed coat is still partly recognised. After enough changes a new vaccine is needed. A person's memory is not an antibody. The model shows only that recognition by shape fades step by step.
flow.context: This is the last step of Drift Cards. Here you look at the answers and link them to a virus whose coat changes a little every year.

activities.title: The Knife Trail: how far does one blade carry it?
activities.context: In this activity turmeric on a piece of banana stands for a viroid in one sick plant. You cut that piece and then eight clean pieces with the same butter knife, and count how many pick up the yellow. Viroids travel between plants on cutting tools in this way.

materials.item: ripe bananas
a butter knife, which is not sharp
turmeric powder mixed with a few drops of water into a paste
a plate, a dry cloth, and soap and water

schedule.what: Cut a turmeric-marked piece of banana, then eight clean pieces with the same knife. Count the yellow ones. Repeat after wiping the knife.

activities.record: Draw the row of eight pieces for each run. Colour in the ones that showed yellow on the cut face. Write how many pieces were marked in each run.

setup.art: A plate with eight thick slices of banana in a row and a ninth slice at the left end with bright yellow turmeric paste on its top.
setup.caption: 1. Lay 8 thick pieces of banana in a row. Rub turmeric paste on a ninth piece.

setup.art: A butter knife cutting down through the turmeric-covered banana piece, its blade smeared yellow.
setup.caption: 2. Cut the yellow piece in half. Do not wipe the knife.

setup.art: The same knife cutting the fourth banana slice in a row, with the first three already cut in half and showing yellow streaks on their cut faces.
setup.caption: 3. Cut each clean piece in half, in order. Look at each cut face for yellow.

flow.do: 1. Peel one banana and cut it into 9 thick pieces. 2. Lay 8 of them in a row on the plate. 3. Rub turmeric paste over the top of the ninth piece. 4. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: The yellow piece is a plant with a viroid. The others are healthy plants. The knife will cut the yellow piece first, and then all eight in a row without being wiped. How many of the eight will show yellow? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Cut a banana into 9 thick pieces. Lay 8 in a row. Rub turmeric paste on the ninth. Guess how many of the 8 will turn yellow. Write why.
flow.parent: A butter knife is safe for a child to use on banana. Guesses of one or two are common.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Knife Trail. Here you set out eight clean pieces of banana and one marked with turmeric, and guess how far a knife will carry the yellow.

flow.do: 1. Cut the yellow piece in half, straight down through the paste. 2. Without wiping the knife, cut piece 1 in half, then piece 2, and so on to piece 8. 3. Open each piece and look at the cut faces. 4. Count the pieces that show any yellow.
flow.say: Cut straight down each time, with the same part of the blade. Now open each piece. Which ones show yellow?
flow.kid: Cut the yellow piece in half. Do not wipe the knife. Cut pieces 1 to 8 in order. Open each one. Count the ones with yellow.
flow.parent: Expect clear yellow on the first two or three pieces and a faint trace on a few more. The exact number depends on how wet the paste is.
flow.context: In this step of the Knife Trail you cut a turmeric-marked piece of banana and then eight clean pieces with the same unwiped knife.

flow.do: 1. Wash and dry the knife and the plate. 2. Cut the second banana into 9 pieces and set up again, with fresh paste on the ninth. 3. Cut the yellow piece. 4. This time wipe the blade once on a dry cloth. 5. Cut pieces 1 to 8 and count the yellow ones.
flow.say: This time we wipe the blade on a dry cloth after the yellow piece. Will that be enough? What do you think, and why?
flow.kid: Set up again with the second banana. Cut the yellow piece. Wipe the blade once on a dry cloth. Cut pieces 1 to 8. Count the yellow ones.
flow.parent: A dry wipe usually leaves a faint trace on the first piece or two. If you have banana left, try once more after washing the blade with soap. That should leave none.
flow.context: In this step of the Knife Trail you repeat the cutting test, but wipe the knife on a dry cloth after cutting the turmeric-marked piece.

flow.do: 1. Compare the two drawings. 2. Ask the questions below. 3. Eat the banana. Turmeric is food.
flow.say: A coconut cutter may harvest many palms in a day with one blade. What does your test tell you about that blade?
flow.kid: Compare your two rows. What did wiping change? Now think of a blade that cuts many palms a day. Then eat the banana.

ask.q: Did the yellow reach only the next piece, or further?
good: Further. Several pieces after the first were marked.

ask.q: A viroid is far too small to see. How would a farmer know the blade was carrying them?
good: They would not know by looking.
They would only see sick plants years later.

flow.parent: Turmeric is not a viroid. It stands for something carried on a blade from one cut to the next. A real viroid is copied in each new plant, so a faint trace is enough.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Knife Trail. Here you compare an unwiped knife with a wiped one, and think about tools that carry viroids between plants.

activities.title: Fold It Wrong: one strip of paper, two shapes
activities.context: In this activity you fold the same kind of paper strip into two shapes, a coil and a flat zigzag, and find out which one stacks into a pile. It is a model of the normal shape and the prion shape of one protein.

materials.item: strips of paper, each about 2 centimetres wide and 20 centimetres long
a pencil

schedule.what: Make six paper coils and six flat zigzags from the same strips. Test which shape stacks into a pile. Then refold one coil into a zigzag.

activities.record: Draw one coil and one zigzag. Write how many of each you could stack before the pile fell. Write one sentence on what was added or taken away when you refolded a coil.

setup.art: A paper strip being wound tightly round a pencil, with two finished springy paper coils lying beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Wind 6 strips round a pencil, one at a time, and slide each off. These are coils.

setup.art: A paper strip folded back and forth like a fan and pressed flat, with a neat stack of five such folded strips beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Fold 6 strips back and forth every 2 centimetres and press them flat. These are zigzags.

setup.art: A child trying to balance paper coils on top of each other as they roll away, next to a tidy pile of flat zigzags.
setup.caption: 3. Try to stack the coils. Then stack the zigzags. Which pile stands?

flow.do: 1. Wind one strip tightly round the pencil and slide it off. It is a coil. 2. Make 6 coils. 3. Fold another strip back and forth every 2 centimetres, like a paper fan, and press it flat. It is a zigzag. 4. Make 6 zigzags.
flow.say: Every strip is the same paper, the same length. Only the folding is different. Which shape do you think will stack into a pile? Why?
flow.kid: Wind 6 strips round a pencil to make coils. Fold 6 strips back and forth to make flat zigzags. Guess which shape will stack. Say why.
flow.parent: The coil stands for the normal shape of the PrP protein, which is mostly coils. The zigzag stands for the prion shape, which is flat sheets.
flow.context: This is the first step of Fold It Wrong. Here you make six paper coils and six flat paper zigzags from identical strips.

flow.do: 1. Try to stack the 6 coils on top of each other. Count how many stay. 2. Stack the 6 zigzags, each lying on the one below. Count how many stay. 3. Blow gently on each pile.
flow.say: Stack the coils. Now stack the zigzags. Blow on both. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Stack the coils. Count how many stay up. Stack the zigzags. Count again. Blow gently on both piles. What happens?

ask.q: Why do the zigzags stack and the coils roll away?
good: The zigzags are flat, so each one lies on the next.
The coils are round and springy, so they touch at only one small place.

flow.parent: The zigzags make a neat pile that stays. The coils roll off after one or two.
flow.context: In this step of Fold It Wrong you test which paper shape, coil or flat zigzag, stacks into a pile that stays.

flow.do: 1. Take one coil. Press it flat against the top zigzag of the pile and fold it along the same creases. 2. Add it to the pile. 3. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: You have turned a coil into a zigzag. Did you add any paper? Did you take any away? What changed?
flow.kid: Press one coil flat against a zigzag. Fold it the same way. Add it to the pile. Did you add or remove any paper?

ask.q: What was added or taken away when the coil became a zigzag?
good: Nothing. It is the same strip.
Only the shape changed.

ask.q: In this model your hands did the refolding. What does it in a nerve cell?
good: The prion itself, when it touches a normal protein.

check.q: A prion and the normal protein beside it differ in what?
options: The amino acids they are made of
check.why: A prion has the same chain of amino acids as the normal protein, folded another way. Neither carries any genes. If you chose amino acids, remember your strips: the paper never changed, only the folds.

flow.parent: A paper model shows three things only: the same chain can have two shapes, one shape stacks, and stacks hold together. It does not show why a real prion makes its neighbour refold.
flow.context: This is the last step of Fold It Wrong. Here you refold a paper coil into a zigzag and ask what changed, as a model of a normal protein becoming a prion.

activities.title: Sleeping Guests: which viruses has my family carried, and for how long?
activities.context: In this activity you ask the grown-ups at home who has had chickenpox, and work out how many years each person has carried that virus. The chickenpox virus stays hidden in nerve cells for life.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil

schedule.what: Ask family members whether and when they had chickenpox or the vaccine. Work out how many years each has carried the virus.

activities.record: Make a table with four columns: the person, chickenpox or vaccine or neither, about which year, and years carried so far. Write 'me' and 'a parent' in place of names.

setup.art: A child with a notebook asking an older woman a question while she shells peas at a table.
setup.caption: 1. Ask each grown-up: did you have chickenpox? About which year?

setup.art: A notebook page with a four-column table and a subtraction sum written beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Take that year away from this year. That is how long the virus has stayed.

flow.do: 1. Your child asks two or three people at home, or by phone, whether they had chickenpox and about which year. 2. Ask about yourself too: chickenpox, the vaccine, or neither. 3. Write the answers in the table.
flow.say: Ask whoever you like. Did they have chickenpox? About what year? Nobody has to answer if they would rather not.
flow.kid: Ask two or three grown-ups: did you have chickenpox? About which year? Write the answers in a table. Add yourself.
flow.parent: Most adults who grew up in India had chickenpox as children. Many children today have had the vaccine, which is offered by private clinics. Your child's vaccination card will show it as varicella.
flow.context: This is the first step of Sleeping Guests. Here you ask your family who has had chickenpox and when.

flow.do: 1. For each person who had chickenpox, take that year away from this year. 2. Write the answer in the last column. 3. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: The chickenpox virus does not leave when the spots heal. They stay in nerve cells beside the spine. How many years has each person carried them?
flow.kid: For each person, take the chickenpox year away from this year. Write the number of years. Who has carried the virus longest?

ask.q: The virus is there but the person is well. What keeps the virus quiet?
good: The body's defenders.
Memory cells and other defenders keep watch for the whole of life.

ask.q: Why does shingles come more often in old age?
good: The defences are slower then.
The watch is weaker, so the virus can wake.

flow.parent: About one person in three gets shingles at some time, mostly after sixty. An adult shingles vaccine exists. This activity is for wondering and not for worry.
flow.context: This is the last step of Sleeping Guests. Here you work out how many years each person in your family has carried the hidden chickenpox virus.

projects.title: Four Rules, Four Days: my own takeover trial
projects.context: In this four-day project you run the Factory Test again with one rule changed each day. In the Factory Test a tumbler of plain and marked grains is a model of a cell with a virus in it. At the end you write a one-page report.

materials.item: the grains, tumbler and bowl from the Factory Test, with 64 grains already marked
a notebook and a pencil
squared paper for graphs

schedule.what: Run the basic Factory Test twice. See how much chance changes the result.
A faster virus: every marked grain gets two copies each round.
The cell fights back: take out two marked grains each round. Start with 1, 3, 4 and 5 marked grains.
Test a rule of your own. Write a one-page report.

projects.record: Your report has five parts on one page: my question, my guess and my reason, my table, my graph, and what I found. Add one sentence on what the model leaves out.

setup.art: A steel tumbler of pale and marked grains beside a notebook page headed 'Day 1' with two small tables.
setup.caption: 1. Each day, run the Factory Test with one rule changed. Write a table.

setup.art: A hand taking two marked grains out of a tumbler and setting them aside before adding new ones.
setup.caption: 2. On day 3 the cell fights back: take out two marked grains every round.

setup.art: A one-page report with a question at the top, a table, a line graph with two lines, and three sentences at the bottom.
setup.caption: 3. On day 4, write a one-page report with a table and a graph.

flow.do: 1. Run the basic Factory Test for 7 rounds: 20 plain grains, 1 marked grain, 6 draws, and doubling. 2. Run it again in exactly the same way. 3. For each run, write the round in which 3 or more marked grains were first drawn.
flow.say: Nothing is changed between these two runs. Will they give the same result? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Run the basic Factory Test twice. Change nothing. Write the round when you first drew 3 or more marked grains. Were the two runs the same?
flow.parent: The two runs often differ by one round. This shows how much is chance, and so how big a difference must be before it means anything.
flow.context: This is day 1 of Four Rules, Four Days. Here you run the Factory Test twice with nothing changed, to see how much the result varies by chance.

flow.do: 1. Start with 20 plain grains and 1 marked grain. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason. 3. After each round, add two marked grains for every marked grain in the tumbler. 4. Stop when the pile of marked grains runs out.
flow.say: This virus is copied faster. Each message gets two copies a round. How many rounds sooner will it take over? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Today each marked grain gets two copies each round. Guess how much sooner the virus takes over. Write why. Run it until your marked grains run out.
flow.parent: The marked grains go 1, 3, 9, 27. The pile runs out when the fifth round would need 81. Most runs reach 3 marked draws in round 3 or round 4.
flow.context: This is day 2 of Four Rules, Four Days. Here you run the Factory Test with a virus whose messages triple each round, where before they doubled.

flow.do: 1. New rule: each round, after the draw, take out 2 marked grains. Then double what is left. 2. Run it starting with 1 marked grain. 3. Run it again starting with 3, then 4, then 5. 4. For each start, write the marked grains after each round for 5 rounds. No drawing is needed today.
flow.say: Now the cell fights back. It destroys two virus messages every round. Which starting numbers will the cell clear? Guess first, and say why.
flow.kid: New rule: take out 2 marked grains each round, then double the rest. Try starting with 1, 3, 4 and 5. Which starts does the cell clear?

ask.q: What happened with a start of 4?
good: It stayed at 4 for ever.
Take out 2 leaves 2, and doubling gives 4 again.

flow.parent: A start of 1 is cleared at once. A start of 3 goes 3, 2, 0. A start of 4 stays at 4. A start of 5 goes 6, 8, 12, 20 and grows. So the number of viruses that get in matters, which is true of real infections too.
flow.context: This is day 3 of Four Rules, Four Days. Here the model cell in the Factory Test destroys two virus messages each round, and you test different starting numbers.

flow.do: 1. Your child invents one new rule and writes a question about it. 2. Your child writes a guess and a reason, and then runs the test. 3. Your child writes the one-page report.
flow.say: What rule would you like to test? Write your question first, then your guess and your reason. Then run it.
flow.kid: Invent one new rule. Write your question, your guess and your reason. Run the test. Write your one-page report.
flow.parent: Good rules to suggest if your child is stuck: the virus removes two plain grains each round, or the cell starts fighting back only from round 4.
flow.context: This is day 4 of Four Rules, Four Days. Here you test a rule of your own on the Factory Test and write a one-page report.

challenges.title: Which Part Shall We Show? Plan a vaccine for a made-up virus
challenges.context: This is a design challenge on paper. A made-up virus called virus K has appeared, and you plan a vaccine against them. You must choose which kind of vaccine to make, and no kind is best at everything.
challenges.problem: Virus K is made up. They have a spike on the outside that fits a receptor in the human throat, a coat protein under a fatty envelope, and an RNA genome. The spike changes a little every year. The coat protein hardly changes, but it is hidden inside. Plan a vaccine. Decide what to show the body, and how.
constraints: It must be safe for a newborn baby and for an old person whose defences are weak.
It must keep in an ordinary fridge. Many health centres have no deep freezer.
It should need as few doses as possible.
A new version must be ready within a year if the spike changes.
general: A whole inactivated virus. It is safe for weak defences and keeps in a fridge. It needs several doses, and growing a lot of virus takes time.
A live weakened virus. One or two doses are enough. It is not given to people whose defences are very weak.
creative: The spike alone, made by yeast cells that have been given the spike gene. It is very safe and keeps in a fridge, but it needs boosters.
A message of mRNA for the spike. A new version can be made in weeks. The first mRNA vaccines needed very cold freezers.
Show the body the coat protein that hardly changes, as well as the spike. Then the vaccine may still work after the spike drifts.
Use two kinds: a quick one in the first year, and a longer-lasting one once there is time to make it.
challenges.your_turn: Draw a table with your four constraints across the top and three kinds of vaccine down the side. Put a tick or a cross in each box. Choose one plan and write two sentences on why. Then write the one thing your plan does badly. Every real vaccine has one.

setup.art: A large drawing of a made-up round virus with outer spikes, a fatty envelope, a coat underneath and a coiled genome inside, each part labelled.
setup.caption: 1. Draw virus K and label the spike, the envelope, the coat and the genome.

setup.art: A hand-drawn table with four column headings and three rows, some boxes ticked and some crossed.
setup.caption: 2. Test each kind of vaccine against the four constraints with ticks and crosses.

setup.art: A child's one-page plan with a chosen vaccine circled and two sentences written under it.
setup.caption: 3. Choose one plan. Write why, and what it does badly.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem and the four constraints aloud. 2. Your child draws virus K and labels the four parts. 3. Ask which part the body's antibodies can reach.
flow.say: Which parts of virus K are on the outside? Which part can an antibody touch on a whole virus particle?
flow.kid: Read the problem. Draw virus K. Label the spike, the envelope, the coat and the genome. Which part can an antibody touch?

ask.q: Why can antibodies reach the spike and not the coat protein?
good: The spike is on the outside.
The coat is hidden under the envelope.

flow.context: This is the first step of Which Part Shall We Show? Here you read about a made-up virus called virus K and draw their parts.

flow.do: 1. Your child lists the kinds of vaccine they know. 2. For each kind, ask what it would show the body. 3. Read the usual solutions aloud only after your child has tried.
flow.say: What kinds of vaccine could we make? For each one, what exactly would the body see?
flow.kid: List the kinds of vaccine you know. For each one, say what the body would see. Then read the usual solutions.
flow.parent: The four kinds are a live weakened virus, a whole inactivated virus, one part, and instructions for one part. Let your child name as many as they can first.
flow.context: In this step of Which Part Shall We Show? you list the kinds of vaccine that could be made against the made-up virus K.

flow.do: 1. Draw the table: four constraints across, three kinds of vaccine down. 2. Fill each box with a tick or a cross. 3. Your child chooses a plan and writes why.
flow.say: No kind gets four ticks. Which crosses can you live with? Why?
flow.kid: Draw the table. Put a tick or a cross in every box. Choose one plan. Write two sentences on why.
flow.parent: There is no single right answer. A strong answer names what was given up, such as 'more doses, but safe for everyone'.
flow.context: In this step of Which Part Shall We Show? you test three kinds of vaccine against four constraints and choose a plan.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child that the spike of virus K has now changed in three places. 2. Ask what happens to their plan. 3. Ask what they would do next.
flow.say: A year has passed. The spike has changed in three places. Does your vaccine still work? What would you do now?
flow.kid: A year has passed. The spike has changed in three places. Does your plan still work? What would you do next?

ask.q: Which plans cope best with a changed spike?
good: One that can be remade quickly, like mRNA.
One that also shows a part that hardly changes.

flow.context: This is the last step of Which Part Shall We Show? Here the made-up virus K changes their spike, and you decide what to do with your vaccine plan.

challenges.title: The Wet Road: wrap a message so that it arrives
challenges.context: This is a building challenge. You write a short message in sketch pen on thin paper and wrap it so that it survives under water. The mRNA in a vaccine is just as fragile, and it travels inside a tiny bubble of fat.
challenges.problem: Write a five-word message in sketch pen on a piece of thin paper about 5 centimetres square. Wrap it so that it can stay under water for 30 seconds and still be read. The person who receives it must be able to open it with their fingers.
constraints: The message must be written in sketch pen, which runs in water.
The wrapped message must fit inside a matchbox.
The wrapper must open by hand in under 10 seconds, with no scissors.
You may use at most three kinds of material.
materials: a little cooking oil or ghee
pieces of an old plastic bag
general: Wrap the message tightly in a piece of plastic bag and tie it with thread.
Fold it inside foil and press the edges shut.
creative: Rub a thin layer of ghee or oil all over the folded paper. Fat and water do not mix, so the water stays out. The real vaccine uses a bubble of fat.
Rub wax crayon hard over both sides of the paper before folding it.
Use two layers: fat on the inside and foil on the outside, so that a hole in one does not matter.
Fold the paper so that the writing is in the middle and the outer folds take the water.
challenges.your_turn: Build your own wrapper and test it three times with a fresh message each time. Count how many of the three could be read. Then change one thing and test again. Write which wrapper was best, and what a fat bubble does for the message in a vaccine.

setup.art: A small square of thin paper with five words written on it in sketch pen, beside a matchbox for size.
setup.caption: 1. Write five words in sketch pen on thin paper about 5 centimetres square.

setup.art: A child's hands folding the small paper and rubbing ghee over it from a steel spoon, with foil and a piece of plastic bag nearby.
setup.caption: 2. Wrap it your own way. It must fit in a matchbox.

setup.art: A wrapped parcel held under water in a steel bowl with a spoon, and a child counting on a clock.
setup.caption: 3. Hold it under water for 30 seconds. Unwrap it by hand. Can you read it?

flow.do: 1. Write five words in sketch pen on a scrap of thin paper. 2. Dip it in the bowl with no wrapper for 5 seconds. 3. Look at it together. 4. Read the problem and the constraints aloud.
flow.say: Look at what the water did in five seconds. A message of mRNA breaks down about as easily in the body. How could we get this message through the water?
flow.kid: Write five words in sketch pen. Dip the paper in water for 5 seconds. What happened? Now read the problem.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Wet Road. Here you see what water does to an unwrapped message written in sketch pen.

flow.do: 1. Your child plans a wrapper with at most three materials. 2. Your child builds it and checks that it fits in the matchbox. 3. Read the usual solutions only after the first try.
flow.say: Choose up to three materials. Which ones keep water out? How will the other person open it?
flow.kid: Plan your wrapper. Use up to three materials. Build it. Check that it fits in the matchbox.
flow.parent: Let the first design fail if it will. Tissue paper wrapped only in more paper soaks through at once, and that is useful to see.
flow.context: In this step of the Wet Road you plan and build a wrapper that will keep a paper message dry under water.

flow.do: 1. Hold the wrapped message under water with a spoon for a slow count of 30. 2. Take it out and open it by hand. Time the opening. 3. Read the message. 4. Test three fresh messages and count how many could be read.
flow.say: Thirty seconds under water. Then open it with your fingers. Can you read every word?
flow.kid: Hold it under water for a count of 30. Open it by hand. Can you read all five words? Test three times.
flow.parent: Plastic tied with thread usually leaks at the knot. A fat layer works well but makes the paper see-through, and the words can still be read.
flow.context: In this step of the Wet Road you test your wrapped message under water for 30 seconds, three times.

flow.do: 1. Your child changes one thing and tests again. 2. Compare the two designs. 3. Talk about the fat bubble in an mRNA vaccine.
flow.say: Change one thing only. Was it better? In the vaccine, the fat bubble also has a second job. It merges with the cell's fatty membrane and lets the message in. Does your wrapper have a second job?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Test again. Which design was better? Why does the vaccine's message travel in fat?

ask.q: Why is fat a good wrapper for a message that must get into a cell?
good: Fat keeps water and enzymes away from the message.
A cell's membrane is fatty too, so the bubble can merge with it.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Wet Road. Here you improve your wrapper and compare it with the fat bubble that carries the mRNA in a vaccine.

worksheets.title: Takeover, the quiet gap, vaccines, prions and viroids

items.p: Who builds the new virus proteins in an infected cell?
items.why: A virus particle has no ribosomes. The cell's ribosomes build every virus protein, from the virus's messages. White blood cells fight viruses and do not build them.

items.p: A virus breaks into a cell by force and then builds copies of themself.
items.why: False. A virus builds nothing. Their coat fits a receptor, the cell takes them in, and the cell's ribosomes do all the building.

items.p: Put the seven steps of a virus in a cell in order, from first to last.
items.why: The virus attaches to a receptor, enters and loses their coat. The cell's ribosomes read the virus's messages and the genome is copied. New particles assemble and leave.

items.p: The time between a germ getting in and the first sign of illness is the ____ period.
items.why: During the incubation period the virus is being copied in a growing number of cells, but too few are infected for the person to feel ill.

items.p: In the Factory Test, why did you draw more marked grains in the later rounds?
opts: The rules told you to pick them
Marked grains are easier to feel
There were more marked grains to pick
items.why: The marked grains doubled each round, so a blind pick landed on them more often. Nothing forced the pick. A ribosome meets virus messages more often for the same reason.

items.p: Match each way of carrying on to a virus who does it.
pairs: Hide in nerve cells for years
Join the DNA of a bacterium
items.why: Polio viruses burst the cell. Flu viruses bud out wrapped in the cell's membrane. The chickenpox virus hides in nerve cells. Lambda phage can join the DNA of E. coli and wait.

items.p: A person can pass on a cold before they feel ill.
items.why: True. The virus is copied for a day or more before enough cells are infected for the person to notice. New particles are already leaving the nose in that time.

items.p: What does a vaccine show the body?
opts: A medicine that kills the germ
A wall the germ cannot cross
The illness in a mild form
items.why: A vaccine shows the body an antigen, which is a part of the germ that defenders recognise by shape. It is not a medicine or a wall. Most vaccines cause no illness at all.

items.p: Sort these vaccines by what they show the body.
items: One part, or instructions for one part
One part, or instructions for one part
cats: One part, or instructions for one part
items.why: Measles vaccine and oral polio drops hold living, weakened viruses. Covaxin and the injected polio vaccine hold whole viruses that cannot be copied. The hepatitis B vaccine holds one protein, and an mRNA vaccine holds the message for one protein.

items.p: A wrongly folded protein that makes normal proteins fold wrongly too is called a ____.
items.why: A prion has the same chain of amino acids as the normal protein, in another shape. It has no DNA or RNA.

items.p: What is a viroid made of?
items.why: A viroid is a loop of RNA a few hundred letters long, with no coat. A protein with no genes describes a prion. DNA in a coat describes some viruses.

items.p: Explain why you feel well for a day or two after a cold virus gets into your nose.
items.a: At first only a few cells are infected. The virus must be copied through several rounds of cells before many are infected. Only then do the body's alarm signals make me feel ill.
items.why: A strong answer says that the virus is present and being copied the whole time, and that there are too few infected cells at first to notice.

items.p: Draw a ribosome with a cell's message and a virus's message. Show what the ribosome builds from each.
items.a: The drawing shows the same ribosome building a cell protein from the cell's message and a virus protein from the virus's message.
items.why: A ribosome builds from any message with the right starting signal. It builds a virus protein in the same way as one of the cell's own.
items.art: A blank box with a small two-part ribosome drawn in the middle and two empty strands beside it.

items.p: Draw a virus particle with a spike, a coat and a genome. Label each part and write what it does.
a: Spike: fits a receptor on the host cell
Coat: protects the genome outside a cell
Genome: the instructions that the cell copies and builds from
items.why: The spike decides which cells the virus can enter. The coat protects the genome. The genome is the only part that carries instructions.

items.p: A girl has chickenpox at seven. At seventy she gets shingles. Where was the virus for 63 years?
items.a: The virus stayed hidden in nerve cells beside her spine. Her body's defenders kept them quiet. In old age the virus woke and travelled down one nerve to the skin.
items.why: A strong answer says that the virus never left the body, names nerve cells, and says the virus woke when the defences were weaker.

items.p: A polio virus blocks the cell's own messages. Why are polio messages still read?
opts: They start in a different way
items.why: The cell's messages need a cap at the front for a ribosome to start. Polio messages have a folded stretch that lets a ribosome start without a cap. Ribosomes read both kinds of message in the same way.

items.p: Flu viruses cut the caps off the cell's messages and use them on their own.
items.why: True. This is called cap snatching. The cell's message is ruined, and the flu message now carries a cap that ribosomes accept.

items.p: What does interferon do to the cells near an infected cell?
opts: It makes them slow their protein building
items.why: Warned cells slow their ribosomes and cut up RNA, so a virus who enters them gains little. Antibodies come later, from B cells.

items.p: Many bacteria store pieces of phage DNA in a row called ____.
items.why: The stored pieces let the bacterium recognise the same phage later and cut that phage's DNA. The row is copied at each division, so the daughters inherit it.

items.p: Match each defence to the step of the virus that it stops.
items.why: Antibodies cover the spikes so the virus cannot attach. Interferon slows the ribosomes that read. The RNA cutter destroys genomes being copied. A killer T cell destroys the cell before particles leave.

items.p: Why is the flu vaccine changed every year?
opts: Old vaccine goes bad in storage
The body forgets in a year
Flu is a new virus each year
items.why: Copying mistakes change the flu virus's spikes a little each year, and old antibodies fit less well. It is the same family of viruses, slowly changing.

items.p: A vaccinated person can never be infected by that virus.
items.why: False. A vaccine gives a head start. The virus may enter some cells before antibodies stop the spread, so the person is ill mildly or not at all.

items.p: Put in order what happens after an mRNA vaccine is given.
items: The fat bubble merges with a cell
B cells that fit the spike multiply
a: The fat bubble merges with a cell
B cells that fit the spike multiply
items.why: The message gets into a cell inside a fat bubble. Ribosomes build the spike from it. Defenders that fit the spike multiply, and some remain as memory cells.

items.p: Three of these diseases have a vaccine. Which one does not?
items.why: Colds are caused mostly by rhinoviruses, and at least 165 types are known. Antibodies against one type give little protection against the rest.

items.p: Two doses of measles vaccine protect for many years. A flu vaccine protects for about one. Explain the difference.
items.a: The measles virus's antigens hardly change, so the same memory cells keep fitting. The flu virus's spikes drift a little every year, so old antibodies fit less well and a new vaccine is needed.
items.why: A strong answer is about the virus changing or not changing. The body's memory lasts in both cases.

items.p: A rinsed lump of curdled milk did not curdle fresh milk. What does this show?
opts: A changed protein rarely passes its change on
Lemon juice does nothing to milk
items.why: In Lemon, Chhena or Nothing, the lemon changed the milk and the lump did not. In ordinary proteins a changed form is not catching. A prion is unusual because its changed form is.

items.p: A virus and a prion both get 'copied'. Say what is copied in each case.
items.a: In a virus, the genome is copied, and new coat proteins are built from it. In a prion, nothing is built. Normal proteins already in the cell are refolded into the prion's shape.
items.why: A strong answer says that a virus passes on instructions and a prion passes on a shape.

items.p: Here are three views about what an infected cell is.

views.says: It is a sick cell. The virus is an invader, and my job is to stop them.
It is the virus in their living form. The particle outside is only the travelling stage.
It is one living cell following two sets of instructions at once.

items.ask: Which view fits best with what you saw in the Factory Test? Give one reason.
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a view and uses the test. For example: the cell biologist's view fits, because my tumbler held both kinds of message and I built from both.
items.why: Real scientists hold each of these views. The facts are agreed, and the argument is about which words describe them best.

items.p: Draw two line graphs of virus numbers over six days: one for a person with a vaccine, one without.
items.a: Without a vaccine the line stays low for a day or two, rises high and falls after antibodies arrive. With a vaccine the line begins to rise and is turned down early, staying low.
items.why: Memory cells make antibodies within days, during the quiet gap. So the virus is stopped while there are still few infected cells.
items.art: Two empty graphs side by side, each with 'Days 1 to 6' along the bottom and 'Number of viruses' up the side.

items.p: Sort these by whether a ribosome ever reads them.
items.why: Virus messages and vaccine mRNA are read by ribosomes, which build proteins from them. A viroid is copied by an enzyme but never read. A prion is a protein and holds no message.

worksheets.title: Models, memories and things that copy with almost nothing

items.p: In the Factory Test, a cell with twice as many plain grains was taken over only one round later. Why?
opts: Doubling catches up in one round
items.why: The marked grains double every round. So going from 20 to 40 plain grains costs the virus just one more doubling. This is why a virus who is copied quickly is hard to outrun.

items.p: The Factory Test's model cell had no defences. Name one real defence. How would you add it?
items.a: One answer: interferon and RNA-cutting enzymes. I would take out two marked grains every round before copying. Another answer: antibodies. I would stop the marked grain from going into the tumbler on a die roll of 3 to 6.
items.why: A strong answer names a real defence and gives a rule that could be carried out with grains and a die.

items.p: Rule: take out 2 marked grains, then double the rest. What does a start of 5 do?
items.why: 5 take away 2 is 3, and doubled is 6. Then 6 gives 8, and 8 gives 12. One extra grain at the start tips the balance. In a real infection, too, the number of viruses that get in matters.

items.p: Ribosomes read a viroid's RNA to build the viroid's coat.
items.why: False. A viroid has no coat and no gene for any protein. A plant enzyme copies the RNA loop, and no ribosome ever reads it.

items.p: Between 3 and 8 percent of human DNA came from ____ who joined our ancestors' DNA.
items.why: Retroviruses write a DNA copy of their genome into the host's DNA. When this happened in egg or sperm cells long ago, the virus DNA was inherited.

items.p: Vaccinating people ended smallpox. Why can it not end rabies in the same way?
opts: Rabies is caused by a prion
Rabies virus also lives in other animals
items.why: Smallpox infected only humans, so breaking the human chain ended the virus. Rabies virus is also copied in dogs, bats and other animals. Rabies does have a good vaccine.

items.p: Put in order how a prion spreads inside a brain.
items: The pile grows and breaks into pieces
A prion touches a normal protein
Each piece refolds more normal proteins
The normal protein refolds and joins the pile
a: A prion touches a normal protein
The normal protein refolds and joins the pile
The pile grows and breaks into pieces
Each piece refolds more normal proteins
items.why: A prion works by touch. Each refolded protein joins the pile, the pile breaks, and every piece starts a new pile. No genome is copied at any step.

items.p: Match each one to what it passes on.
items.why: A bacterium divides into two whole cells. A virus passes on a genome packed in a coat. A viroid passes on RNA alone. A prion passes on only a way of folding.

items.p: Hepatitis D virus borrows the outer proteins of hepatitis B virus. Why does the hepatitis B vaccine protect against both?
items.a: Hepatitis D virus can be copied and can spread only in a person who also has hepatitis B virus, because they use hepatitis B's outer proteins. The vaccine stops hepatitis B, so hepatitis D has nothing to borrow.
items.why: A strong answer says that hepatitis D depends on hepatitis B. Stopping the one stops the other.

items.p: Smallpox virus is kept frozen in two laboratories. Here are three views on what to do.

views.says: Destroy the samples. An escape would be a disaster, and nobody is vaccinated now.
Keep them. If a similar virus appears, we may need them to test new medicines.
Ending a kind of being for ever is a serious act. We should at least keep the record.

items.ask: Which view do you find strongest? Name one risk of the view you chose.
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a view and names its risk. For example: keep them, but the risk is an accident or a theft.
items.why: This argument is real and has gone on for decades. Each view protects something that matters and risks something else.

items.p: Draw a bacterium's CRISPR row. Show what happens when a phage whose piece is stored attacks again.
items.a: The drawing shows a row of short stored pieces in the bacterium's DNA, a guide copied from one piece, and a cutting protein using the guide to cut the matching phage DNA.
items.why: The stored piece is copied into a guide. The cutting protein carries the guide and cuts any DNA that matches it.
items.art: A blank outline of a rod-shaped bacterium with a circular chromosome inside and a phage standing on the outside.

items.p: Lambda phage usually waits inside a starving bacterium and does not burst out. What could the phage gain?
opts: A starving cell makes few new phages
items.why: A starving cell has little material and energy, so few phages would be made. Joined to the cell's DNA, the phage is copied at each division until times are better.

items.p: A mouse with no gene for the PrP protein cannot get prion disease.
items.why: True. A prion spreads by refolding normal PrP. With no normal PrP in the body, the prion has nothing to refold.

items.p: Why is a bubble of fat a good wrapper for the mRNA in a vaccine? Give two reasons.
items.a: Fat keeps water and RNA-cutting enzymes away from the fragile message. A cell's membrane is fatty too, so the bubble can merge with it and let the message in.
items.why: A strong answer gives one reason about protection and one about getting into the cell.

items.p: Three of these are built by your own ribosomes. Which one is not?
opts: The spike after an mRNA vaccine
items.why: Covaxin holds whole virus particles that were grown in a factory and inactivated. The other three are all built inside your body by your ribosomes.

quiz.p: What does a virus bring into a cell?
quiz.why: A virus brings a genome, which is a set of instructions. The cell supplies the ribosomes, the energy and the amino acids. If you chose ribosomes, remember that a virus particle has none.

quiz.p: Why does a cell build proteins for a virus?
opts: Ribosomes build from any message they meet
The virus pays the cell with energy
quiz.why: A ribosome builds from whichever message it meets. Once virus messages are in the cell, they are read like the cell's own. No force is used.

quiz.p: Why is there a quiet time after a virus gets in, before a person feels ill?
opts: The virus has not entered any cell
Too few cells are infected at first
quiz.why: The virus is being copied from the start, but it takes several rounds of cells before many are infected. If you chose 'asleep', that describes a latent virus, which is a different thing.

quiz.p: The chickenpox virus leaves the body when the spots heal.
quiz.why: False. The virus stays hidden in nerve cells for life. Decades later they can wake and cause shingles along one nerve.

quiz.p: Which defence starts within hours, long before antibodies are made?
quiz.why: An infected cell releases interferon at once, and the cells nearby slow their protein building. New antibodies take one to two weeks the first time. Antibiotics do not act on viruses.

quiz.p: How does a bacterium recognise a phage who attacked their ancestors?
opts: From a stored piece of the phage's DNA
quiz.why: The bacterium keeps a short piece of the phage's DNA in a CRISPR row and uses it as a guide for cutting matching DNA. Bacteria have no blood and no antibodies.

quiz.p: Which kind of vaccine holds whole virus particles that can no longer be copied?
quiz.why: In an inactivated vaccine the whole virus is treated so that the genome cannot be copied, and the shape remains. A live weakened virus can still multiply a little.

quiz.p: What do your cells build after an mRNA vaccine?
quiz.why: The mRNA is the message for one protein, such as the spike. Ribosomes build only that. The message does not enter the nucleus and does not change DNA.

quiz.p: Why is there no vaccine against the common cold?
opts: Colds are too mild to matter
At least 165 types of cold virus exist
quiz.why: Antibodies against one type of rhinovirus give little protection against the others. A vaccine would have to cover a very large number of types.

quiz.p: A virus who infects only humans could be ended for good by vaccination.
quiz.why: True. Such a virus needs an unbroken chain of human hosts. Smallpox was ended this way in 1980, and wild polio is close to its end.

quiz.p: How does a prion spread in a brain?
quiz.why: A prion has no genes and does not divide. It touches a normal protein of the same kind, and that protein takes the prion shape. If you chose genes, you were thinking of a virus.

quiz.p: Which of these is a bare loop of RNA with no coat?
quiz.why: A viroid is RNA alone. A prion is protein alone. A phage is a virus, with a genome in a coat, and a bacterium is a whole cell.

quiz.p: Which of these did the Factory Test leave out?
quiz.why: The model cell never fought back. A real cell senses virus RNA, sends out interferon and may self-destruct. The model did include the cell's messages, the copying and chance.

applications: Vaccine makers choose which part of a virus to show the body. The hepatitis B vaccine shows one surface protein, made by yeast cells.
mRNA vaccines can be redesigned in weeks when a virus's spike changes, because only the message has to be rewritten.
Doctors give medicine for shingles within three days of the rash, because it works by stopping the virus's DNA from being copied.
Health workers in India mark a child's little finger with ink after polio drops, so that no child is missed on an immunisation day.
Farmers and plant nurseries clean their cutting tools between plants, because viroids and some plant viruses travel on blades.
Hospitals use extra-strong cleaning for instruments that have touched brain tissue, because ordinary heat does not destroy prions.
Many countries do not allow cattle to be fed meal made from other cattle and sheep, to keep prions out of the food chain.
Scientists use the CRISPR system of bacteria as a tool to cut DNA at a chosen place. A treatment for sickle cell disease is made this way.

open_questions.q: Can a vaccine be made against HIV?
open_questions.why_open: HIV changes faster than flu and hides inside the white blood cells that organise the defence. Many vaccines have been tested since the 1980s and none has protected well enough.

open_questions.q: What is the normal PrP protein for?
open_questions.why_open: It sits on nerve cells in every mammal, so it is probably useful. Mice without it live, with some problems of movement and memory. Its exact job is not known.

open_questions.q: Can prion disease be cured or stopped?
open_questions.why_open: There is no treatment yet. Researchers are testing ways to make the body produce less normal PrP, so that prions have less to refold. Nobody knows yet whether this will work in people.
They may be left over from a time before cells, or they may have escaped from plant RNA much later. They leave no fossils, so the question is hard to test.

open_questions.q: Do prion-like proteins help to store memories?
open_questions.why_open: Some experiments in sea slugs, fruit flies and mice suggest that a self-copying protein shape helps keep a memory at a nerve junction. It has not been shown in humans.

open_questions.q: Can one flu vaccine be made that works against every flu virus, every year?
open_questions.why_open: It would have to show the body a part of the virus that cannot change. Several such vaccines are being tested, and none is in use yet.

ask_kids: The cell built the viruses, and the virus only sent the instructions. So who made them?
Which written instructions did you follow today without knowing who wrote them?
You sneezed today, but the virus got in two days ago. What was happening inside you yesterday?
Who in our family is carrying the chickenpox virus right now, quietly?
Why do you think the same vaccine works for a baby in Kochi and a baby in Kohima?
If you could look at any part of a virus to teach your body, which part would you choose, and why?
A prion passes on a shape. Can you think of anything else that passes on a shape and nothing more?
Is it fair that Katalin Karikó was demoted while she was doing the work that later won a Nobel Prize?
A coconut palm can be killed by 246 letters of RNA. What is the smallest thing you know that causes a big change?

jokes.a: It had been taking orders from a virus all day.

jokes.j: Why are prions so bad at origami?
jokes.a: They fold it the wrong way, and then everybody copies them.

jokes.j: What is a viroid's favourite thing to wear?
Why does the flu virus need a new photo every year?
What did the antibody say to the virus?
Knock, knock. Who's there? Chickenpox. Chickenpox who?
Why did the vaccine get top marks?
jokes.a: It always did the revision before the test.

jokes.j: What do you call a virus who is never on time?
Why did the ribosome get into trouble?
jokes.a: It never checked who was sending the messages.

maths.problem: In the Factory Test, the marked grains start at 1 and double every round. How many are in the tumbler in round 7? How many had to be taken from the store?
maths.answer: 64 marked grains. 63 came from the store.
maths.explain: The numbers go 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64. Round 7 has 64. The first one was there at the start, so 64 take away 1 is 63 grains from the store. The store began with 70, which leaves 7.
maths.context: This is about the Factory Test. In it, marked grains stand for a virus's messages in a model cell, and they double every round.
maths.why_maths: A doubling pattern tells you how many grains to prepare, and shows why the store nearly runs out.

maths.problem: In round 5 of the Factory Test the tumbler holds 16 marked grains and 20 plain grains. What fraction is marked? About how many of 6 draws do you expect to be marked?
maths.answer: 16 out of 36, which is 4 ninths. About 2 or 3 of the 6 draws.
maths.explain: 16 and 20 make 36 grains. 16 out of 36 is 4 out of 9, because both divide by 4. Four ninths of 6 is 24 divided by 9, which is about 2.7. So expect 2 or 3 marked grains, though chance can give 1 or 4.
maths.context: This is about the Factory Test. In it, you draw 6 grains without looking from a tumbler of plain and marked grains.
maths.why_maths: A fraction tells you what to expect from a blind draw, so you can tell an ordinary result from a surprising one.

maths.problem: With 20 plain grains, the marked grains first outnumber the plain ones in round 6. With 40 plain grains, in which round does this happen? Why is it not round 12?
maths.answer: Round 7. Doubling needs only one more round to pass a number twice as big.
maths.explain: The marked grains go 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64. 32 is more than 20, so that is round 6. 64 is more than 40, so that is round 7. Each round multiplies by 2. So making the cell twice as big costs the virus one extra round, and not twice the rounds.
maths.context: This is about the Factory Test, run once with 20 plain grains and once with 40. The marked grains double every round.
maths.why_maths: Comparing doubling with a fixed number explains why a bigger cell hardly slows a virus down.

maths.problem: One cell infected with polio virus can release up to 10,000 particles. Suppose every particle infected a new cell, and each of those released 10,000. How many particles is that? Why does this not happen in a body?
maths.answer: 100,000,000 particles, which is one hundred million. In a body, most particles never reach a cell.
maths.explain: 10,000 times 10,000 is 100,000,000. Count the zeros: four and four make eight. In a real body, most particles are trapped in mucus, break down, or are covered by antibodies. So the real number is far smaller, but the sum shows how fast the number could grow.
maths.context: This is about burst size, which is the number of new virus particles that one infected cell releases.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying by a burst size shows why a body must respond within days, and why a head start from a vaccine matters.

maths.problem: Rule: take out 2 marked grains, then double what is left. Start with 5 and write the next four numbers. Which starting number stays the same for ever?
maths.answer: 5, then 6, 8, 12, 20. A start of 4 stays at 4.
maths.explain: 5 take away 2 is 3, doubled is 6. Then 4 doubled is 8, 6 doubled is 12, and 10 doubled is 20. For a number to stay the same, taking away 2 must leave exactly half of it. Half of 4 is 2, and 4 take away 2 is 2. So 4 stays at 4.
maths.context: This is about day 3 of Four Rules, Four Days. In it, a model cell destroys two virus messages each round, and the rest double.
maths.why_maths: Following a rule step by step finds the tipping point between an infection that is cleared and one that grows.

maths.problem: Two doses of measles vaccine are about 97 percent effective. If 200 vaccinated children all met the measles virus, about how many might still fall ill? With one dose, about 93 percent effective, how many?
maths.answer: About 6 children with two doses. About 14 children with one dose.
maths.explain: 97 percent protected leaves 3 percent. 3 percent of 200 is 6. With one dose, 7 percent are left unprotected, and 7 percent of 200 is 14. So the second dose more than halves the number who fall ill.
maths.context: This is about how well the measles vaccine works after one dose and after two doses.
maths.why_maths: Turning a percentage into a number of children shows what a second dose is worth.

maths.problem: A Drift Card is a 3 by 3 grid, and each square is shaded or blank. How many different patterns are possible? How many of them differ from your card 0 in exactly one square?
maths.answer: 512 patterns. 9 of them differ from card 0 in exactly one square.
maths.explain: Each of the 9 squares has 2 choices. So there are 2 times 2, nine times over, which is 512. To differ in exactly one square, you change one of the 9 squares, so there are 9 such patterns.
maths.context: This is about Drift Cards. In it, a pattern of shaded squares on a 3 by 3 grid stands for the coat of a virus that changes a little each year.
maths.why_maths: Counting the patterns shows how many different coats even a tiny grid allows, and how few are close to the one the body learned.

maths.problem: In Seven Steps or Stopped, a defence card stops the virus on a roll of 3, 4, 5 or 6. What is the chance that it works? What is the chance that it fails twice in a row?
maths.answer: 4 out of 6, which is 2 thirds. It fails twice in a row 1 time in 9.
maths.explain: Four of the six faces stop the virus, so the chance is 4 out of 6, or 2 thirds. It fails on 1 or 2, which is 1 third. Failing twice is 1 third of 1 third, which is 1 ninth.
maths.context: This is about the card game Seven Steps or Stopped. In it, the body plays a defence card and a die decides whether the virus is stopped.
maths.why_maths: Chances show why a good defence still fails now and then, and why a second layer of defence helps so much.

maths.problem: The cadang-cadang viroid is 246 letters long. A polio virus genome is about 7,500 letters. About how many times as long is the polio genome?
maths.explain: 246 is close to 250. 7,500 divided by 250 is 30. So the genome of one of the smallest viruses is about 30 times as long as this viroid.
maths.context: This is about the sizes of genomes. A viroid is a bare loop of RNA, and a polio virus is one of the smallest viruses.
maths.why_maths: A ratio makes it clear how little a viroid has, even compared with a very small virus.

warmup.q: Who builds the new viruses in an infected cell?
warmup.a: The cell does. Its ribosomes build virus proteins from the virus's messages.

warmup.q: Why do you feel fine for a day or two after a cold virus gets in?
warmup.a: Too few cells are infected at first. The virus needs several rounds of copying before you notice.

warmup.q: Name three things a virus can do after entering a cell.
warmup.a: Burst out, bud out, or stay hidden.

warmup.q: What does a vaccine show the body?
warmup.a: An antigen, which is a part of the germ that the body's defenders recognise by shape.

warmup.q: Why does the flu vaccine change every year?
warmup.a: The flu virus's spikes drift a little each year, so old antibodies fit less well.
A wrongly folded protein that makes normal proteins of the same kind fold wrongly too.
A bare loop of RNA with no coat, found only in plants.

warmup.q: What signal does an infected cell send to the cells nearby?
warmup.a: Interferon. The neighbours slow their protein building.

warmup.q: Where does the chickenpox virus go after the spots heal?
warmup.a: Into nerve cells beside the spine, where they stay hidden for life.

quiz: A virus particle has ribosomes of their own.
A virus has none. The host cell's ribosomes do all the building.
A person can pass on a cold before they feel ill.
The virus is being copied for a day or more before any sign shows.
The chickenpox virus stays in the body for life.
They hide in nerve cells and can wake decades later as shingles.
A prion carries a small genome.
A prion is only protein. What it passes on is a shape.
Viroids infect humans.
Viroids have been found only in plants.
An mRNA vaccine changes your DNA.
The message is read by ribosomes and then broken down. It does not enter the nucleus.
Interferon is made by the virus.
The infected cell makes it, to warn the cells nearby.
Smallpox has been ended everywhere in the world.
It was declared eradicated in 1980.
Cooking destroys prions.
Prions survive cooking, which is one reason they are hard to deal with.
Bacteria can keep a record of the viruses who attacked them.
The record is a row of stored DNA pieces called CRISPR.
odd: The first three are viruses with a genome. A prion is a protein with no genome.
The first three are live weakened vaccines. Covaxin is an inactivated vaccine.
The first three are defences of the body. A spike is part of a virus.
The first three are steps of a virus in a cell. Dividing in two is what a bacterium does.
The first three can stay hidden in the body for years. A cold virus is cleared in about a week.
