how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that a protein alone can pass on a disease? This card tells the true story of prions, and of a rule that turned out to be too strict.
how_we_found_out.story: Scrapie is a brain disease that passes from sheep to sheep. In the 1960s every biologist was sure that a slow virus caused it, because anything that is copied and passed on must carry DNA or RNA. Tikvah Alper, a scientist born in Cape Town, led a radiation laboratory at Hammersmith Hospital in London. She knew that ultraviolet light and radiation wreck DNA and RNA. She gave scrapie material doses that would have destroyed any virus. It could still infect. In 1967 she published the result in the journal Nature under a title that was a question: does the agent of scrapie replicate without nucleic acid? In the same years John Griffith showed on paper how a protein alone could do it. The idea was met with astonishment, and few accepted it. In 1982 the American doctor Stanley Prusiner purified the scrapie agent and found protein and nothing else. He named it a prion. He was attacked for years. In 1997 he received the Nobel Prize.
how_we_found_out.who: Tikvah Alper, a radiobiologist in London. John Stanley Griffith, who worked out how a protein could be copied by shape. Stanley Prusiner, an American doctor and biochemist.
how_we_found_out.when: Alper's paper was published in 1967. Prusiner named the prion in 1982 and received the Nobel Prize in 1997.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That scrapie was caused by a slow virus, and that nothing can be copied and passed on without DNA or RNA. Alper showed that the scrapie agent survived treatment that destroys DNA and RNA.

roots.context: We have run a model cell with grains and learned how a virus, a vaccine, a prion and a viroid each get copied or built. Now we ask what this tells us about being open to the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Factory Test, you built whatever each grain said, and never asked who had sent it. A cell's ribosomes build in this way too. So a virus takes over a cell without any force, using only a message. An mRNA vaccine gets in by the same opening. What lets a cell be robbed is also what lets a cell be taught.
deep_truth.habit: We think of an infection as an attack by force, and of safety as a wall that keeps things out. But a virus brings no force at all. Building from messages is how a cell does everything, and every protein in your body was built that way. A cell that built from no new message could not be infected, and could not be vaccinated either. So being open and being in danger are not two separate things that we can pull apart.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Factory Test, one marked grain among twenty plain ones took half of the jobs or more within five or six rounds, and nobody was forced. One polio virus particle becomes up to 10,000 in four to six hours, all built by the cell. An mRNA vaccine and a virus both work because ribosomes build from whatever message they meet. The body stays safe by checking what was built afterwards, with interferon, antibodies and memory cells. If your own Factory Test came out differently, write down what you got and run it again.

three.who_am_i: You are a being who can be changed by what you take in. That is how a virus makes you ill. It is also how a vaccine protects you, and how you learn anything at all.
three.what_is_life: A living cell builds from messages. Some of those messages are the cell's own, some arrive from outside, and some that arrived long ago are now part of the cell's genome.
three.what_is_this_world: A very small thing with the right shape or the right message can redirect the work of a very large thing. One loop of RNA 246 letters long can kill a coconut palm.

roots.thread: A virus particle on their own does nothing that we can see. A cell alone builds only more cell. When the two meet, one message is read thousands of times and becomes thousands of particles. So the many new viruses come from one message and one cell's work, together. Neither of them made the viruses alone.

teachings.teaching: Whatever is said, and whoever says it, wisdom is to find out what is true in it.
teachings.link: A ribosome builds from every message it meets. Thiruvalluvar says a wise mind does one thing more: it weighs the message itself, whoever sent it. The body's defenders do something like this when they check each new protein by its shape.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha tells the people of a town not to accept a teaching only because it is repeated, handed down, written in a text, or spoken by a respected teacher. They should accept it when they have seen for themselves that it leads to good and not to harm.
teachings.link: A cell that has met a virus keeps a record of the result, in memory cells or in a CRISPR row. Next time, the same message is judged by what it led to before. The Buddha asks people to judge teachings in the same way, by what they lead to.

science.text: Ribosomes build proteins from virus messages and from the cell's own messages by the same steps. This is why viruses can be copied in cells and why mRNA vaccines work.
Between 3 and 8 percent of the human genome came from viruses who joined the DNA of our ancestors, and at least one of their genes is used in the placenta.

Viruses sense the state of their host and act on it. Lambda phage bursts out of a well-fed cell and waits in a starving one. Some scientists call these automatic chemical switches and would not call them decisions.

other_view.view: They would say that words like 'open', 'robbed' and 'taught' are human stories laid over chemistry. A ribosome and a message meet by chance, and they fit or they do not. Nobody is trusting anybody. On this view the lesson of the virus is practical: learn the steps, and block one. Many would add that a virus is not alive, and so is not a someone at all.

practice.title: Whose message is this?
practice.say: Sit still with your hands in your lap. Close your eyes. Breathe in slowly and breathe out slowly, five times. Now wait. Soon a small message will arrive. It may say 'scratch your nose' or 'open your eyes' or 'move your foot'. Do not do it yet. Notice the message first. Ask quietly: who sent this? Then decide whether to do it. Wait for three messages in this way. Then open your eyes.
practice.kid: Sit still. Close your eyes. Breathe slowly five times. Now wait for a message. It may say 'scratch' or 'move'. Do not do it yet. Notice it first. Ask: who sent this? Then decide. Do this three times.

ask: A cell's ribosomes build from any message with the right start. Is that a weakness in the cell, a strength, or both? Why?
The cell did all the building, and the virus supplied only the instructions. So who made the new viruses?
In the practice, a message arrived and you waited before doing what it said. Where do you think those messages come from?
A virus can stay in a body for sixty years, and virus genes have been in human DNA for millions of years. When does a guest become part of the house?

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game and challenge was reasoned through step by step for a family in a city flat. None has yet been tried at home, so treat the amounts and times as a starting point. The Factory Test (the main investigation) needs about 110 pale grains, a pen and a steel tumbler. Marking 63 grains takes time, which is why the first run is given 28 minutes. The chances were worked out by arithmetic: with 20 plain grains, the first round with 3 or more marked draws is most often round 5, and often round 4 or 6. With 40 plain grains it is most often round 6, and about 1 run in 20 does not get there in 7 rounds. The child must take the first grain touched and not feel for a mark, and a pen mark cannot be felt. Lemon, Chhena or Nothing needs a grown-up for the hot milk. The lump must be rinsed for a full 30 seconds, or leftover lemon may curdle a little of tumbler B, and the step says what to do then. A skin on hot milk is not curdling. This test shows what a prion is not, because nothing in a kitchen can show a prion at work. Whose Note Is It? works best on someone who has not seen the page. Drift Cards depends on the person tested, and people vary. In the Knife Trail, how many pieces turn yellow depends on how wet the turmeric paste is. A butter knife is safe on banana. Seven Steps or Stopped was played 20,000 times by a short computer program with the rules as written: the Virus wins about 49 games in 100 with no vaccine and about 22 in 100 with one. Three games are few, so a family may see something different. In the Wet Road, plastic tied with thread usually leaks at the knot. Four Rules, Four Days reuses the marked grains. Nothing needs a garden. Facts checked online on 19 Nov 2026, mostly against Wikipedia articles and the sources they cite: the polio virus numbers (up to 10,000 particles a cell, 4 to 6 hours, about 7,500 letters), lambda phage (about 100 phages at about 50 minutes, the choice between bursting and waiting), Esther Lederberg's finding, Ellis and Delbrück 1939, cap snatching in flu, interferon 1957, CRISPR (Barrangou 2007, the 2020 Nobel Prize), Katalin Karikó's story, measles and flu vaccine figures, the 165 rhinovirus types, the hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis D, Covaxin, Covishield, Rotavac, the polio dates for India, smallpox, shingles, the share of virus DNA in the human genome and syncytin, prions (Alper 1967, Prusiner 1982 and 1997, PrP, the mice without PrP), kuru, mad cow disease, viroids and cadang-cadang, Thirukkural 423 and Anguttara Nikaya 3.65. Not checked against a source this time, and written from general knowledge: that new antibodies take one to two weeks the first time, the incubation times of a cold and chickenpox, that the measles virus's coat tolerates little change, that the first mRNA vaccines needed very cold freezers, the examples of medicines on the defence cards, the yeast prion that changes which sugars a cell uses, that E. coli can divide every 20 minutes, that smallpox samples are kept in two laboratories, the Tamil word akki for shingles, and the journal details of some papers in the sources list. A person should check these. The story is made up, and its medical facts are real.
